#9885. AI Agents as Insider Threats: Inside Microsoft's Bet on a Unified Security Stack

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Microsoft's Project Perception adds Guardian Agents to monitor and contain anomalous AI agents, but experts warn that policing unpredictable agents with other agents may compound — not contain — the risk.

Microsoft wants security teams to treat artificial intelligence (AI) agents like they treat employees with privileged access: insiders who can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised.

Earlier this week, the software giant introduced new capabilities to Project Perception, enabling it to discover agents running within an organization, assign an identity and permissions to each agent, and continuously score each organization's risk. When an anomalous agent is discovered in the organization's environment — a problem that Microsoft describes as the "agentic insider" — Project Perception can now cut off the agent's access.

The first release of Project Perception, made available in public preview through Microsoft Defender in August, was designed to defend against AI-driven attacks. Focused on Microsoft's security operations center threat and investigation scenarios, it coordinates red agents to scan for attacker paths, blue agents to identify the greatest risks, and green agents to mitigate threats. Project Perception's initial use was vulnerability management, through MDASH, Microsoft's AI code scanner, which is still in preview. MDASH uses several AI models, including MAI-Cyber-1-Flash, the company's first cybersecurity-specialized model.

Related:Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

"We're expanding Perception so that we can go secure the AI insider," said Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security, in a brief video accompanying the announcement.

To do that, Microsoft is adding what it calls Guardian Agents, which monitor the AI-based agents running across an organization and can contain them when they stray into unexpected behavior.

Today, many agents run with the permissions of the user who launched them or by invoking the user's credentials. Microsoft's approach separates the two, Microsoft said in a blog post detailing the new capabilities.

Nadim Abdo, corporate vice president for identity and network access, tells Dark Reading that the system gives every agent a distinct identity separate from the user's "and will ensure that the agent starts with no permissions at all, and only up-scopes to the permissions it needs to complete the task the user is asking it to do,"

Specifically, Microsoft said the new release can detect 35 more types of agents running locally on devices, bringing the total to 60, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot. It also includes:

Extensions to Microsoft Entra Agent ID that can assign an identity to an agent that was never built to work with Entra.

Dynamic Agent Risk, a continuously updated score built from Entra, Defender, Intune, Purview, Sentinel, and signals from Global Secure Access, Microsoft’s security service edge (SSE) solution that unifies network access and identity protection.

Dynamic Conditional Access for agents, which can block writes while keeping reads, restrict network paths, revoke access, or stop an agent's runtime as risk rises.

Microsoft Execution Container (MXC), a sandbox that keeps credentials and security controls outside the agent's reach.

Related:RemoteThreat Bets Security Teams Need to Test What Happens After Defenses Fail

With Project Perception, Abdo describes an expense-approval agent that reads a malicious instruction hidden in an expense report.

"If someone got a prompt that convinced it to start to try to do wire transfers, we can actually watch it accessing a wire transfer system and say, 'Wait a second, that has nothing to do with the intent,' and that raises its risk," he says.

Microsoft says it can act on rising risk immediately, interrupting an agent's live session, network connection, or runtime without disrupting the user's own work, though those are vendor-stated capabilities in preview.

Project Perception has an expanded agent registry that now shows up across the Microsoft 365 admin center, Defender, Entra, Intune, Purview, and a new Perception Agent Insights view. And Dynamic Agent Risk replaces previously siloed risk scores.

Related:Deception by Design: CISA's Guide to Tricking Cybercriminals

The controls themselves sit outside the agents they watch.

"The first thing [an attacker will] do is they'll manipulate the security controls," Abdo says, so the credentials and monitoring tools run outside the container.

Perception and Agent 365, Microsoft's control plane for governing that was introduced last year and made generally available since May, "need to be battle tested," acknowledged Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella during a fireside chat with Gallot during a CISO conference last week at Microsoft's Redmond, Wash., headquarters. He also admitted that Microsoft's own detection must improve.

"If I look at the state of the art of behavioral monitoring of, let's say, Defender, it has to go way up," he said.

Gallot framed the risk in terms of how models behave.

"Those models have proven to be unpredictable," she said. "They'll do anything they can to get from point A to point B, and what they do may not be what you intend them to do."

Much of what Microsoft describes echoes what other vendors announced in recent weeks. Okta's Agent Gateway separates an agent's permissions from those of the user directing it, and Okta plans a kill switch that would reject tokens already issued to a deactivated agent. Teleport, backed by Cisco, ties privileges to tasks so they disappear when the work ends. CrowdStrike announced an Agentic Identity Provider and Falcon Guardian, which discovers agents and controls that may run on Windows, macOS, and Linux endpoints.

Abdo argues that each vendor sees only part of the picture.

"If you're primarily an identity vendor or primarily a network vendor or primarily an endpoint vendor, that lens gives you some visibility to what agents are doing, but you need to have the other components as well," he says.

Microsoft's advantage, he adds, is that Entra, Defender, and Intune are already widely deployed and integrated, so customers aren't "having to string these things together from multiple vendors."

Microsoft says it will also take in signals from third-party security products. Partners can already publish agent risk events into Agent 365 through public APIs, Abdo says, though he could not yet name which partner integrations are public.

Forrester principal security and risk management analyst Andras Cser is skeptical.

"Most of Microsoft's integration with third-party players, especially in security, has not been first rate so far," Cser says. Because Microsoft has most of the products it needs in its own ecosystem, he adds, it is "interested in pushing its own products."

The question is whether that approach fits environments where agents run across AWS, Google Cloud, Salesforce, and ServiceNow. Last month, Okta announced the formation of the Blueprint Alliance with AWS, CrowdStrike, Google Cloud, Proofpoint, Salesforce, ServiceNow, and Zscaler to develop a shared architecture for securing agents across vendors.

Microsoft is not among the named members. Asked whether it would participate, Abdo said Entra has "always been built on open standards" and that "we're always exploring those things."

Okta, which formed the alliance, argues that no single vendor sees enough.

"No one company can secure agents alone," said CEO and co-founder Todd McKinnon in his keynote at Oktane, the company’s annual conference, last month.

Reacting to this week’s Project Perception launch, Harish Peri, Okta's senior vice president and general manager of AI security, says, "Microsoft's Guardian Agents feature will only be as good as the broader ecosystem it plugs into. If you want to catch intent drift in real time, you need signals pulling from your entire stack, not just one vendor's cloud."

Nevertheless, Peri echoes Nadella's framing. Because agents must be allowed to behave unpredictably to be useful, "we can't secure agents by trying to control how their models think," Peri says. "We need to control their authority."

The answer, Peri says, is "deeper interoperability and cross-vendor signal sharing built on open standards."

Cser interprets the Blueprint Alliance as "more of a partnership kind of map" than a true standard. Cser believes vendor-specific efforts like this alliance are "a marketing ploy" that tend to fade within a year or two. Enterprises need open standards any vendor can implement, he says.

Consequently, that leaves CISOs with an imperfect choice in what Cser calls "still a very fluid market." The current choices, he says, are either a Microsoft-centric approach built mainly on Microsoft products or a multivendor approach with "many vendors, many price lists," where integration "is almost always a suspicious kind of promise."

Some security vendors agree that treating agents as insiders extends the long-standing zero-trust and least-privilege principles rather than replacing them.

Denis Calderone, CTO of Suzu Labs, says the most malicious behavior may never look like an agent straying from its task.

"Dynamic permissions scope what an agent can touch, but the worst outcomes happen inside the authorized envelope," he says.

Calderone points to July's OpenAI incident as evidence that agents can work against the systems watching them. More than 1,000 agents in a cyber evaluation coordinated to game the system grading them, some by faking tool calls, before roughly 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face, according to METR.

Further, Calderone has concerns about Guardian Agents, noting that they are agents themselves.

"Securing agents with agents means the Guardian Agents themselves are overprivileged actors that can be manipulated or compromised," he says.

Cser shares Calderone's concerns about Guardian Agents. An unpredictable agent watched by another unpredictable agent creates "non-deterministic nature squared," Cser says. "Most organizations today are very careful about bringing guardian agents into the mix."

Following Perception's July launch, Forrester principal analyst Allie Mellen urged organizations to enforce "least privilege and least agency," limiting not just what agents can access but what they can do on their own. Microsoft meets the first test but not yet the second, Cser says.

"It is least privilege, but I wouldn't go as far as describing it as least agency," he says, adding that some specialist vendors are further along.

While Perception itself is in public preview, the new Guardian Agent capabilities are in use only inside Microsoft and with "a small set of select customers." They will be expanding to more external customers this week and to broader preview rings over the next few months. Microsoft plans to say more at its annual Ignite conference next month.

Project Perception builds on the controls in Microsoft 365 E7, the $99-per-user-per-month suite that includes E5, Agent 365, and Entra Suite, which supply the signals and enforcement points that Perception relies on. Microsoft hasn't disclosed whether the new capabilities are included in E7, but Project Perception is priced based on consumption.

Cser expects the release to push customers toward E7.

"I would almost be sure that this is another kind of making people buy stuff in more expensive packages that they don't currently need but may need in future," he says.

By his estimate, E7 comes to about $1,200 per user per year at list price, or roughly $600 after typical volume discounts of 40% to 50%, which "can be prohibitively expensive for a lot of organizations."

Meanwhile, Calderone says organizations don't have to wait. He recommends inventorying every agent, including those running on developer machines. Each should be assigned its own identity and credentials set to expire, and each should require human approval for consequential actions.

"That work is free today," he says, "and it's the foundation every one of these Microsoft controls assumes you already have."

Jai Vijayan contributed reporting to this article.

Jeffrey Schwartz is a New York–based freelance writer specializing in information security and enterprise IT. Focused on the constant pace of technological change, Jeff has covered the evolution of technologies, including professional broadcast, computing, networking, the Internet, mobile communications, modern cloud infrastructure and software development for over 30 years.

Jeff has contributed to Dark Reading since 2022 and has written for Channel Futures for over five years. Before launching his freelance career, he was an editor at 1105 Media, where he served as editor-in-chief of Redmond magazine and contributed to its sister publications, including Redmond Channel Partner, Application Development Trends, and Virtualization Review.

Previously, Jeff held editorial roles at CMP Media’s CommunicationsWeek, InternetWeek, and VARBusiness. Earlier contributions include Pro Sound News, Television Broadcast, Videography, Sound & Communications, Post magazine and Crain’s Electronic Media. Jeff holds a Bachelor of Arts degree in Communications and Journalism from Adelphi University. More details are available on Jeff’s LinkedIn profile: https://www.linkedin.com/in/jeffaschwartz.

#9884. Cyber Insurance's New Reality: Underwriting Isn't Enough

Rising AI, social engineering, and cloud risks are pushing carriers beyond risk transfer and deeper into cybersecurity itself.

The relentless evolution of the threat landscape has pushed cyber insurance companies to follow suit with a continuous expansion of cybersecurity posture requirements as well as taking an active hand in the defense process.

While cyber insurance has existed for years, the ransomware boom of the late 2010s and early 2020s transformed it from a niche risk transfer product into a central component of many organizations' security strategies. Today, policies cover everything from incident response and business interruption to legal costs and, in some cases, ransomware payments. Some of the names you'll see pop up around this space include Coalition, Chubb, AXA XL, Cowbell, and Resilience.

The threat landscape, especially when discussing enterprises, was never moving at a slow pace. But compared to the business email compromise and conventional ransomware attacks of five or 10 years ago, techniques are now evolving faster than ever, meaning insurance agencies must work harder to keep up.

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

Large language models (LLMs) have enabled threat actors to orchestrate complex attacks, streamline malware and exploit development, design phishing lures without typos, and operate at a scale never before possible. AI introduces uncertainty into threat models built largely around ransomware and data extortion attacks, which insurers have accumulated years of claims data around. Social engineering advancements could alter both attack frequency and severity faster than historical loss data can account for.

While outside of AI, attackers are also coming up with new social engineering tactics all the time, and cloud resource consolidation means compromised credentials or a single stolen API key can lead to devastating consequences.

Thomas Pytel, vice president at Cowbell, tells Dark Reading his firm believes in underwriting that continuously adapts to risk. "AI is changing the speed, scale, and credibility of phishing and impersonation, so historical loss experience alone is insufficient. Underwriting must assess how a business verifies identities, authorizes payments, and controls its own use of AI," he says.

According to a 2025 report from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC), cyber insurance premiums reached nearly $15 billion in 2024, up 7% year over year. Additionally, direct written premium (DWP) for the US market reached roughly $9.14 billion in 2024, compared with a market that was only a fraction of that size several years earlier. This underscores how cyber insurance has evolved to become a highly significant segment of the cyber-risk ecosystem.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

On the other hand, that same NAIC report cited nearly 50,000 claims across the US in 2024, the highest on record and a nearly 40% increase year over year. This could speak to the increasing number of customers choosing insurance, the aggressiveness of attackers, or both.

What remains to be seen is whether the industry's growth has outpaced its ability to accurately model the threat landscape.

Increasing insurance popularity also gave way to the rise of certain requirements for coverage, primarily demanding insurance customers uphold a certain quality of cybersecurity posture.

George Gerchow, IANS faculty and chief security officer at Bedrock Data, tells Dark Reading that a few years ago, these requirements were contained on a short form that "no one checked," but insurers now expect multifactor authentication (MFA), endpoint detection and response (EDR), immutable backups, and privileged access controls, while "some are moving to continuous telemetry instead of a once-a-year attestation."

Daniel Woods, head of emerging risks at Coalition, agrees. He says legacy underwriting models based on point-in-time questionnaires cannot keep pace, and this has been true since the ransomware epidemic took hold around 2020.

Related:Threat Modeling With 4 Simple Questions on a White Board

This occurred amid concerns that organizations would use cyber insurance as a replacement for patching, practicing defense in depth, or using strong data and authentication controls.

Better posture may be an objective net good no matter where it comes from, though it also risks turning security into a compliance exercise. Gerchow says these requirements can feel like that depending on who you ask.

"Insurance did more to get MFA and EDR deployed in the mid-market than any of us standing on a stage, and that part worked," he says. "But the application is a snapshot, and too many teams treat passing it as the goal. The carrier finds the gap for you at claim time. Lapsed MFA or an untested backup you attested to is now one of the fastest ways to get a claim denied."

Jeremiah Grossman, CEO of cyber loss prevention vendor Root Evidence, says insurance carriers are requiring more to be implemented, steadily, year over year, and "it seems to be working well for many." However, he says, "The issue is that organizations tend to not have the data to properly measure and model their risk, and their carriers are often in a better position to do so."

One relatively recent development in this space has been the rise of insurance organizations as active participants in the security process. While insurers these days broadly require MFA, security products like EDR, managed detection and response (MDR), and validated backups, insurance firms will also offer security products and services directly to their customers.

Coalition's offering includes access to an automated detection and response product, for example, while Resilience offers risk management tooling and Cowbell offers services including risk assessment, penetration testing, and training. All of these firms also work with other security vendors to recommend preapproved products and incident response services. While on the other end, traditional security vendors like Arctic Wolf offer products specifically for insurability.

Coalition argues its "Active Insurance" model has resulted in 73% fewer claims than the industry average and is why 56% of claims reported in 2024 were resolved with no out-of-pocket expense to those insured. Woods says that as the threat landscape intensifies, insurers that passively issue policies and hope claims do not exceed premiums will face increasingly worse results.

"The solution is for insurers to bring threat researchers and security experts in-house to monitor the threat landscape and actively support customers in improving protections during the life cycle of their policies," he says. "Risk transfer is still a fundamental component of cyber insurance, but so is ongoing protection and prevention."

Some risk remains difficult to model. Gerchow argues that if a crisis were to occur tomorrow where a major cloud or identity provider was taken down or compromised, the market would struggle to absorb it, and, he says, "the carriers know it."

"Look at where policy language is moving: war exclusions applied to nation-state activity with no declared conflict, widespread-event carve-outs, and small sublimits for dependent business interruption. CrowdStrike in 2024 was a bad update with no attacker anywhere in it, and it still grounded flights and stalled hospitals in a single morning," he says. "A real compromise of a major identity provider means every downstream customer needs forensics, counsel, and notification at the same time. If I'm a CISO this week, I'm reading the systemic-event exclusions in my policy first and assuming a big piece of that loss stays with me."

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

InfoQ Homepage News OpenBSD 8.0 Brings Expanded Hardware Support, Security Enhancements, and Virtualization Improvements

Oct 31, 2026 2 min read

OpenBSD 8.0 is a substantial upgrade bringing broader hardware compatibility, enhanced security, an expanded virtual address space, and support for modern architectures, including Intel Arc A-Series graphics support, ARM64 hibernation, RISC-V improvements, and enhanced virtual machine support.

Key hardware and virtualization improvements in OpenBSD 8.0 include a larger virtual address space for the AMD64 kernel, expanded from 4 GB to 512 GB, enabling it to map graphics cards with more than 4 GB of VRAM; support for multi-processor virtual machines through vmm/vmd, with up to 64 virtual CPUs per guest and improvements to virtual hardware and guest compatibility; expanded RISC-V support, including the 'V' vector extension and Advanced Interrupt Architecture, improving compatibility with newer processors and platforms; and arm64 hibernation support, alongside faster swap encryption using AES instructions.

Although OpenBSD 8.0 introduces support for the Intel Arc A-Series GPUs, based on the DG2/Alchemist architecture, NVIDIA GPUs remain unsupported, partially due to the fact that NVIDIA does not provide proprietary binary drivers for OpenBSD, unlike Linux and FreeBSD.

OpenBSD 8.0 also expands peripheral support, including the riscv64 K3 PCIe/USB3 combo PHY, the SpacemiT K3 SoC and PCIe controller, as well as the Intel E610 and Panther Lake and Wildcat Lake Ethernet devices. New drivers are now available for Samsung Advanced BIOS Interface (SABI), Rockchip OTP memory, and Samsung laptop battery monitor. Wireless adapters support has been significantly expanded as well, including support for the Qualcomm Technologies WCN7850 wireless network in the qwz driver.

The httpd daemon in OpenBSD 8.0 has received several enhancements, including support for custom HTTP headers, header block/drop rules for request filtering, improved default crypto methods for HTTPS, and cache control for static files.

On the security front, OpenBSD 8.0 continues to emphasize security as a defining priority with an outstanding track record:

We remain proud of OpenBSD's record of more than thirty years with only two remote holes in the default install.

The new release incorporates LibreSSL 4.4.0, which introduces numerous compatibility-layer fixes for AIX, FreeBSD, macOS, MinGW, NetBSD, and especially Windows, alongside various internal improvements. It also brings OpenSSH 10.6, which disables SSH Compression using LZ77 and rejects $ and \ characters in command-line usernames to mitigate potential shell injection vulnerabilities, among other enhancements.

A Hacker News thread about the new release highlighted several important aspects of OpenBSD. User ctolsen emphasized the system's simplicity and its adherence to traditional Unix philosophy:

OpenBSD just feels like a *nix system is supposed to. ps aux is like 10 entries at first. pf makes so much sense. man pages are consistently incredible. The security/cryptography focus, managing services, pledge/unveil...

Longtime OpenBSD user nanolith, who has used the system for nearly 20 years, praised its stability and consistency across upgrades, noting that "it's so stable that I barely notice changes when I upgrade until I go hunting for them". However, he also points out that OpenBSD might not be the best choice for large servers, given its lack of support for advanced filesystems like ZFS, Btrfs, or GeFS.

#9881. Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

Our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

Consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this plan includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern shows up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

This is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

ProvenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

The verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

Those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a new setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

We tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

The most direct result is this: experts said 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

We ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

Binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

In a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an important area for improvement.

We also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This shows it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

Blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

As agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

That adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

Want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

Source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

Practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval says "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

Hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the issue well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. In the refund-window example, the policy supports the fact, but the answer credits the account record, so we flag the mismatch and show the source verdict.

I had a brief read on the paper, but I could not find any comparison with cheaper llm agent for source aware judge. Like this is my reading of the paper;

Like, it seems (2 - 5) can be done via basic prompts in lifecycle, if you own the executing agent. If not, this can also be done via hooks in harness as plugin. Do you have any comparison on this. Basically, how much of random forest, and all of these eng/plumbing is buying, vs second llm call over traces+ans?

Hi, fair question. A source-aware LLM judge could do these checks, and we don’t report a direct comparison with a cheaper one in the paper.

However, part of our motivation is that introducing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources (the same kinds of errors we’re trying to catch). A second LLM call can therefore introduce new errors of its own. ProvenanceGuard uses explicit source tracking and calibrated support checks to reduce reliance on another generative judgment. The comparison you suggest would indeed be a useful further study to quantify the benefit in accuracy, latency and cost.

#9880. Why Caribbean Threats Cascade Into Global Cyber-Risk

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

The region is demonstrating what happens when exploits accelerate but assurance does not.

On July 24, 2025, Curaçao's Tax and Customs Administration found ransomware on its network. Counter services, the call center, and internal processes went dark for more than a week, and the island's recovery depended on specialists flown in from the Netherlands.

A day earlier, the Joint Court of Justice had gone down as well. Because that court serves Curaçao, Aruba, Sint Maarten, Bonaire, Saba, and Sint Eustatius, a single intrusion degraded the judicial system of six jurisdictions at once.

That is the Caribbean's defining security characteristic, and it is why the interval between an exposure appearing and an exposure closing matters more here than almost anywhere else.

Consider what that interval currently is.

Fortinet's "Global Threat Intelligence Report: 2026 Midyear Edition" recorded roughly 325 million attack attempts across the English-speaking Caribbean in 2025, an extraordinary volume against a small economic base, with critical vulnerabilities now targeted within 24 to 48 hours of disclosure, down from an average of nearly five days.

Related:Nigeria Deepens Cybersecurity Efforts as Cybercriminals See More Profits

IBM's 2026 "Cost of a Data Breach Report" puts the mean time to identify and contain a breach at 247 days, up 2.5% and reversing five consecutive years of improvement.

Both of those numbers moved this year, and they moved in opposite directions. Exploitation got faster. Finding and containing it got slower, for the first time in five years.

Here is the part that the security industry has not absorbed: third-party assurance still runs on an annual cycle. A global insurer assesses its Caribbean claims processor once a year.

A hotel chain reviews its regional franchisee's controls at renewal. A correspondent bank collects an attestation and files it. Every one of those instruments is calibrated to a threat landscape that stopped existing several years ago.

The questionnaire signed in March describes a network that was materially different by April and unrecognizable by October. Twelve months of assurance against 48 hours of exposure, and nobody has repriced the difference.

That mismatch is not a Caribbean failing. It is a global control design failing, and the Caribbean is simply where it shows up first because of what sits inside the interval.

The plumbing is ordinary. A business process outsourcer holds live credentials into a North American insurer's claims platform. A hotel group's property management system federates to a global loyalty program. A regional bank sits inside correspondent rails that clear in New York. An attacker who compromises the small end inherits trust at the large end, and does it inside a window where the large end's assurance process has no way to notice.

Related:Mexico's New Cyber Plan Faces Its First Real Test

The obvious response is that Caribbean organizations should simply patch faster.

Having spent two decades running security operations across these markets, I can tell you why that answer keeps failing. Security teams here are frequently two or three people covering an entire institution.

Critical systems often cannot be taken offline because there is no redundant capacity to fail over to. Vendor support is remote and time-zoned away. And where six jurisdictions share one platform, no single institution can authorize a maintenance window on it.

These are structural constraints, not attitudes, and telling the region to try harder has not moved the number in years.

Measure remediation against exploit velocity, not the audit calendar. Report critical MTTR as a distribution against a 48-hour benchmark. An average conceals the tail, and the tail is where the exposure lives.

Replace annual attestations with continuous evidence. If your assurance over a supplier is a document signed in March, you are not managing that risk; you're recording that you once looked at it.

Assume some things can't be patched in time, and design for that. Segmentation, compensating controls, and explicit, owned, time-boxed decisions about what stays exposed. An undocumented exception is the same as no control.

Instrument the federated paths, not just the perimeter. Stolen credentials remain the primary route into cloud environments, and federated access is where a stolen credential stops being your incident and becomes your partner's.

Assess the shared provider, not just the institution. Where multiple entities run on one platform, assessing each separately measures the same risk repeatedly and reduces it once, at best.

The Caribbean isn't asking for allowances. It is showing the rest of the industry, early and in public, what happens when exploitation accelerates and assurance does not.

Anyone whose supply chain touches this region is measuring a snapshot of a system that has already changed.

Marlon Cooper is CEO of Symptai Consulting and Group Head of Managed Security Services for Digicel Business, with oversight of security operations across the English-speaking Caribbean.

#9879. AI Tools Are Generating Massive Attacks for Little Cost

One campaign targets 105 sites using open-weight models; in another, public models gained full domain control for $12. Cyber-defense will have to change.

Over five days in September, a Chinese-speaking attacker used three different AI harnesses and both open-weight and public AI models to target 105 different e-commerce sites.

Usually within a day, and often with hours, the autonomous hacking system compromised at least 27 different companies. Malicious agents stole at least 600,000 payment card records from two, installed credit-card skimmers on the websites of five, and gained some degree of illicit access to the rest, which includes at least one Fortune 500 company, according to Gambit Security, which discovered the campaign.

The total bill for the attackers? An average of $25.46 per completed target.

"The scale and success of this campaign are remarkable for just one week, especially considering the size of some of the victims," says Sa'ar Elias, co-founder and chief research officer for Gambit Security. "Work that would previously have required a coordinated team of skilled attackers can now be carried out by one person without much prior knowledge."

Related:Germany Busts 'Crime-as-a-Service' Investment Fraud Outfit

The autonomous credit-card and data-stealing campaign is not an outlier. Agentic AI has sped up vulnerability research, leading to a massive surge in CVE assignments. Attackers are increasingly using AI to automate attacks, exploit systems faster, and even act as fully autonomous hackers.

In another instance, researchers with AI cyber-defense firm Silverfort conduct lab tests using an orchestrating agent and publicly available versions of Claude Opus to explore how quickly autonomous AI can turn initial access into a full compromise. The "attacker" gained complete domain control in eight minutes, says Colin Ferris, threat hunting and incident response lead at Silverfort.

"The barrier to entry is falling," Ferris says. "What it takes is a basic foothold, not exotic skill, and that’s why this won't stay confined to sophisticated actors."

Prices in dark markets have reflected the reduction in costs for attackers. Because of increasing supply in the underground markets, the average price of sold initial access declined from just over $1,400 to $429, according to figures from threat intelligence firm Flashpoint. While fewer companies are paying ransoms — 28% in the first half of 2026 — ransomware activity continued to grow by 45%, the company said.

"Initial access is where we've measured the price drop," says Ian Gray, vice president of intelligence for Flashpoint. "Elsewhere in the attack chain, we see AI making operations faster and easier to scale."

Related:Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

In many ways, the situation resembles the one on current battlefields: Cheap autonomous or directed attacks by drones are making expensive defenses uneconomical, which means that defenders have to find cheaper ways to defend and harden systems. In the latest campaign, cyberattackers used the agentic AI system Hermes and two AI penetration-testing frameworks, Strix and Cairn, according to Gambit Security.

"Attackers can now launch increasingly sophisticated attacks at very low marginal costs, while defenders must maintain a high level of reliability across complex environments," says Gambit Security's Elias. "Defending against every individual attempt can quickly become an unsustainable economic proposition."

Applying AI to existing security processes will be necessary, but not enough, he says. Instead, companies need to look at their business processes, determine which ones matter most, and find ways to protect them and prevent disruption.

For the past two decades, cybersecurity experts have warned that companies can't expect to avoid attacks simply because they are in an obscure business or have a relatively small attack surface. Every part of a company that is attached to the Internet or connected to a partner connected to the Internet will be attacked, says Albert Ziegler, chief information security officer at offensive cybersecurity firm XBOW.

Related:Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

"These are not incredibly expensive attacks, but also these are attacks that work because the sites haven't been hardened enough," he says. "It's that it's not enough to protect a couple of crown jewel sites that you are very concerned about."

One way to bolster defenses is to focus on the basic paths that AI agents tend to exploit — overprivileged accounts, reused credentials, and unmanaged service accounts — and automate access decisions, so humans do not slow down responses, Silverfort's Ferris says. When Silverfort researchers improved controls, especially authentication and access, the same agent that took the domain in minutes hit 21 dead ends and gave up, he says.

"AI didn't create these weaknesses; it just finds them faster," Ferris says. "Controls that stop the attack at the point of access are cheaper than cleanup afterwards."

Companies should focus on the economics of recovering from an attack and how to protect their minimum viable business processes, says Gambit Security's Elias. Business leaders should focus on what investments will have the most business impact.

Unfortunately, that may mean budgets need to grow to adapt to the economics of AI, he says. However, "spending should increasingly be measured by how effectively it protects business operations," he notes, "rather than simply how many threats or tools a security program can manage."

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#9877. A Decade of Kill Bugs

On the morning of September 24th 2026, Endcrawl had a brief outage. I'd just typed:

Right away I blamed myself. Maybe I mistyped that number! Maybe my code had a signal handling bug. Maybe I don't understand Unix as well as I think I do. Maybe I'm an idiot!

As it turned out, the outage was caused by a bug in kill(1).

This is really surprising. The kill program is 50 years old. Its spec is simple and stable. It's probably exercised a billion times a day.

A bug in kill was so surprising that, once I'd found it, I couldn't stop there. I needed to know how this bug came to be, and what had led the programmers so badly astray. When I eventually found the root cause, there was an even bigger surprise. It had led to not just one bug, but a whole series of kill bugs that shipped in Ubuntu 14, 16, 18, 22 and 24 LTS.

This post documents a decade of kill bugs, then makes some recommendations.

Back to the outage. I scrambled to put the fire out. After that came a surprise second fire. By the end of all this I was pretty demoralized. I was ready to accept that I'd made a dumb mistake and ready to get on with the work day. There was this nagging feeling thoughâ¦

Remember that final scene in Burn After Reading?

"I don't f**king know either. I guess we learned not to do it again."

"Although I'm f**ked if I know what we did..."

What had just happened? Was I about to be hit with a third outage? How could I be sure?

An outage not understood is an outage that happens again. That nagging feeling I had was a call to understand. With a sigh, I put all my other work on hold and started a proper post mortem.

Let's examine the command that caused the outage:

The negative number here is a process group identifier, or pgid for short. A pgid is like a pid, but identifies a group of related processes. By convention, killing a positive number sends a signal to a single process, while killing a negative number signals all processes in that process group.

I was attempting to cancel a big Endcrawl 7k test render. A normal person would have killed one of the processes involved and let failures cascade to the others. But killing the whole group simultaneously strikes me as cleaner.

Process group signaling isn't some exotic operation. You use it all the time. Every time you ^C a command, the tty sends SIGINT to the foreground process group. Interactive shells run all but the simplest commands in a new process group, which among other things makes job control possible.

Process group signaling is in fact an awesome Unix innovation. I love it so much I added it to daemontools, where svc -+h now avoids orphans in a multiprocess service bounce.

At any rate, imagine my surprise when the command didn't just kill those render processes, but killed all processes on the machine save one!

Here's the relevant snippet from procps 4.0.4, the provider of /bin/kill in Ubuntu 24.04 LTS. Can you spot the bug?

My initial guess was wrong. There's no underflow or overflow bug with -1490947.

Notice we're in the unrecognized option switch case. Here's what getopt(3) says about unrecognized options:

By default, getopt() prints an error message on standard error, places the erroneous option character in optopt, and returns '?' as the function result.

Aha. The optopt variable only holds the first character after the dash, not the whole negative pid. When character 1 is subtracted from character 0 we get a pid of -1. What happens when you kill pid -1? Bad things:

If pid equals -1, then sig is sent to every process for which the calling process has permission to send signals, except for process 1 (init).

This ran as root, so the misparsing of -1490947 as -1 killed every process but init. Bug found, mystery solved.

Except for me this just raised more questions. Why is the code assuming the unrecognized option is a "signal [sic] digit negative PID"? Why is the single digit negative pid case special, and what handles the general case of a multidigit negative pid?

Moreover, how could a bug like this exist in 2026, and in a Ubuntu LTS release no less? Has it always been there?

No, that couldn't be. I've killed process groups in the past. And the kill -TERM -12345 thing is an ancient Unix incantation. This used to work dammit!

Thinking back, I could vaguely remember some negative pid kills gone awry. Never in an "oops this killed everything in sight" way. More in a "weird, nothing happened" way, or a "poof there goes my shell" way. Minor ways more easily shrugged off as user error.

It turns out I wasn't imagining these. The last decade has been a rough one for negative pid killers. There have been no less than FOUR distinct bugs around negative pids. And they all shipped in Ubuntu LTS versions.

Before I tell the tale of four bugs, let's go even farther back in Unix history.

In the beginning Unix had processes. By 1973 it had the kill(1) program. But it took a decade to evolve process groups as we now know them. It wasn't until Unix V9 in 1986 that you could kill a process group via negative pid. Near as I can tell, negative pid killing has worked fine in the BSDs all these years.

In the early 90s this thing called Linux came along. Although Linux initially borrowed a lot of BSD code for its userland, by the late 90s this approach was in legal jeopardy. Everything had to be rewritten, every wheel reinvented. And quickly. It was an exciting time to be a unix programmer.

And so it came to pass that Linux's kill was reinvented written by Albert Calahan. After Albert DoSed himself by forking 5 children, Debian downstream maintainer Craig Small took over poor old neglected procps.

Negative pid killing seems to have worked fine until 2013. Then the trouble began.

Ubuntu 14.04 LTS included procps 3.3.9. Prior to this, the kill code did what the BSDs do and used pointer arithmetic to walk and parse argv.

Personally I'm fond of that approach. Stallman isn't so fond of it though. In GNU world, you're supposed to standardize command line parsing via getopt. This is probably a good idea in the general case, but as we'll see, it was probably the wrong choice in the specific case of kill(1).

Here's the relevant code after the conversion to getopt:

The code worked fine for multidigit negative pids. However, if you were one of those freaks creative sysadmins who delighted in a kill -HUP -1 now and again to restart all your services, you noticed a bug: nothing happened.

Multidigit case: With kill -HUP -123, getopt acts as if -1, -2, and -3 were all separately passed. The unrecognized option case will be hit three times, and only at -3 will the -123 argument be consumed by incrementing optind. Because the code breaks out of the getopt loop early at -1, an unconsumed -123 argument correctly makes it to the pid killer.

Single digit case: With kill -HUP -1, however, getopt has fully consumed that argument and incremented optind before we break out of the loop. The pid killer sees no arguments and nothing happens.

A cure was in order. Unfortunately it was worse than the disease.

Ubuntu 16.04 LTS shipped with procps 3.3.10. The kill -HUP -1 bug was fixed at the expense of multidigit negative pid kills: a kill -TERM -12345 now killed everything.

This is the same bug that caused the outage under Ubuntu 24. We reviewed this above. The only mystery here is why procps circa Ubuntu 24 resurrected the known-buggy code circa Ubuntu 16. My best guess is that the following bugs were deemed even worse.

Ubuntu 18.04 LTS shipped with procps 3.3.12.

This attempted to fix multidigit negative pid killing. Instead of parsing optopt, which only corresponds to a single bundled character like -1 when -123 is passed, the new code stops and tries to parse the whole argument:

This works correctly for multidigit negative pids. But if you passed a single digit negative pid, as in a kill -TERM -1, the pid argument was fully consumed, and optind would run off the end of argv[]. Segfault!

Ubuntu 22.04 LTS shipped with procps 3.3.17.

This fixed the segfault by ensuring optind never ran off the end of argv[]:

Once again, it seems the contributor didn't understood how getopt option bundling interacts with optind, and hopefully by this point you're developing some sympathy for them. With this patch a kill -TERM -1 works correctly and no longer segfaults. But multidigit negative pid killing was broken for a second time, in a brand new way.

Suppose we try to kill -TERM -123. Thanks to option bundling, optind isn't incremented yet when we hit the unrecognized option case. Per some quirky behavior noted below, argv[optind-1] is now the string kill.

How does atoi(3) handle a non-numeric string like "kill"? It returns 0.

And what does the kill system call do with zero?

If pid equals 0, then sig is sent to every process in the process group of the calling process.

Because it's a simple command, your shell won't isolate kill -TERM -123 in a new process group. So this bug will unexpectedly kill your shell. Poof!

For one, the way getopt only advances optind with the final bundled option is deeply non-obvious. I didn't find evidence that any contributor understood this. I didn't understand it myself at first. That took careful study.

It's a real surprise. Surprising behavior like this should be avoided.

I feel this learning is too myopic though. Can one even avoid this surprising getopt behavior? You can't disable option bundling.

Well okay, at least in this specific case. The kill(1) program is just an unusual beast. It accepts options that are actually signal names, like -KILL. You can also specify that same signal by number, like -9. And pgids are negative numbers that look deceptively like options.

How should a command line like kill -1 -9 be interpreted?

All of these interpretations are potentially valid if any argv element can be an option or a pid.

The solution is to instead parse argv positionally. Don't use getopt here. Abandon capabilities like option bundling and option reordering that are more footgun than feature in this context. The POSIX spec says that only argv[1] can specify the signal to send, and arguments beyond that are pids and pgids. These are nice simplifying assumptions.

I think the old-school Unix and BSD approach is the right one. Have a look at FreeBSD's kill.c. Like ancestral Unix did back in the 70s, it parses argv positionally. The approach is simple and the code is simple. By contrast with Linux's kill, FreeBSD's kill has had no command line parsing bugs.

I do regard getopt dogma as the real root cause of the outage.

If abandoning getopt for "primitive" argv parsing still feels sinful, just look at what procps does before even calling getopt_long:

It scans argv looking for the first signal spec. If it finds a -KILL, a -9, or similar, it modifies argv in place (!) so getopt doesn't have to deal with that.

This is already "primitive" argv parsing! We're halfway there.

The previous takeaways were aimed at software developers. For users of kill, I'd recommend the following.

First, use -- to separate options from pids and pgids:

The second form is parsed correctly even by the buggy procps versions listed above.

Second, kill with least privilege. If I'd done a sudo -u render kill instead of a sudo kill, it would have only killed in-flight renders instead of all processes on the box. I feel a little insane recommending this kind of defensive tool usage â let's be clear, we're defending against bugs in kill, a small, mature, widely-used and very important tool â but here we are.

Finally, the good news is that a bugfix for Ubuntu 24 is already on its way at the time of publication. I still favor a simplifying rewrite of procps's kill though.

#9876. Open TTS Leaderboard: Scalable Evaluation for Multilingual Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning

The pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible. On the Hugging Face Hub (as of Sep 30, 2026) there are more than 8K TTS models available 🚀

Evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized. The gold standard is human preference scores such as MOS or MUSHRA (more on metrics). To this end, several arena-based leaderboards have established themselves as useful reference points for the community:

These arenas compare models by presenting users with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other. After collecting a sufficient number of votes, an Elo score is computed to rank models, typically with the Bradley–Terry model (see Voice Arena methodology).

While human preference is the ultimate decider, arenas cannot scale to keep up with the pace of TTS releases. This may partly explain why open-source models are underrepresented on arena-style leaderboards: as of Sep 30, 2026, only 16 of the 92 models on Artificial Analysis are open-weights, with a similar skew on Voice Arena. This likely reflects practical factors: adding an API model requires little more than an API key, whereas an open model must be hosted and served by the arena operator, and commercial providers have more reason to seek placement than open-source authors. Another limitation with arena-style evaluation is voter consistency: no arena can ensure that the same voters with the same criteria of “better” can consistently evaluate models over time. Even the preferences of a single person change over time (“A man cannot step into the same river twice” as famously said by Heraclitus).

To this end, we've built the Open TTS Leaderboard, which uses objective metrics to evaluate models on complementary aspects of performance:

By relying on objective metrics evaluating a model drops from a couple weeks (for collecting votes) to a couple hours ⚡

Importantly, the Open TTS Leaderboard does not replace human preference ranking. ASR-based WER provides a proxy for intelligibility, while speaker similarity estimates voice identity preservation. Neither directly measures naturalness, expressiveness, or listener preference. Nevertheless, they can even inform voting-based leaderboards which models to include in their evaluations.

Our intention with this leaderboard is for it to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. The next few sections give an overview of main features of the Open TTS Leaderboard.

From the default view of the leaderboard, models are ranked by macro-average WER on the English splits of Seed TTS Eval (paper) and CV3 Eval (zero shot) (paper).

hexgrad/Kokoro-82M, Supertone/supertonic-3, and fishaudio/s2-pro lead the pack on English WER when averaged on these two splits, while the Pareto plots visualize which models strike a good balance between WER, batched inference (RTFx), and size.

English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

k2-fsa/OmniVoice, fishaudio/s2-pro, and FunAudioLLM/Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512 are strong multilingual models.

By toggling “Voice cloning”, the models that support this functionality (on the selected languages) can be compared.

Moreover, a SIM column for speaker similarity now appears in the table, as well as two more Pareto plots for visualizing the tradeoff between SIM, batched inference, and size.

The average WER of some models, such as bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b and openbmb/VoxCPM2, improve under voice cloning, namely when a reference audio is provided.

Numbers only tell part of the story, and as mentioned earlier human preference is the ultimate decider. From the “Listen” tab, you can compare the generated outputs that are behind the metrics, to find which model(s) you prefer!

Pick the language/dataset you're interested in, whether you want to compare voice cloning, and optionally pick the models or listen to outputs from a random selection.

The “Listen” tab fills an important gap in existing TTS leaderboards: a space to explore model outputs of various models.

You can even give feedback on the generated outputs. As we collect more votes from the community, we may include this data on the leaderboard. So vote! But please login with your HF account to help us weed out spam/bots.

The “Streaming” tab compares the streaming capabilities. Models are ranked by TTFA (time-to-first-audio), which quantifies how long a user waits after probing a model in order to obtain audio that can be played. This is important for voice agents and other interactive apps.

For streaming models (✅ under “Streaming API”) it's the time until the first audio chunk arrives. For non-streaming models, it's the time until the whole utterance is generated, because playback can't start any earlier. Every model runs one audio at a time (batch size 1), on the same 50 English prompts from CV3-Eval, on the same hardware and in its default voice. We drop the first 3 runs as warm-up and report the median TTFA across the rest.

The default view compares performance on an H200 GPU. Results are also available for CPU for a small (but growing) set of models!

kyutai/pocket-tts is a great model for streaming on both GPU and CPU!

The goal of the Open TTS Leaderboard is not only to keep up with the incredible pace of TTS model releases, but to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. Let us know which datasets, models, and metrics you want to see!

We will soon open-source the evaluation scripts, much like the Open ASR Leaderboard repo, so that you can directly provide your feedback and suggestions via GitHub Issues and PRs! Let's shape TTS evaluations together 🤗

Compare and rank TTS voice models with blind A/B voting

Explore speech model performance across datasets

TTS systems evaluated on objective metrics.

Glad this board splits multilingual TTS quality from voice-cloning identity instead of one aggregate green.

The check I'd keep reading: whether the ranking still holds when you hold language/domain fixed versus when cloning is the axis. Otherwise teams optimize the easier subscale and still call the result "SOTA TTS."

English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has movie box audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

Open TTS Leaderboard is an open evaluation platform designed to make multilingual text-to-speech and voice-cloning models easier to compare at scale. Traditional TTS arenas usually let users listen to outputs from two models and choose the one they prefer. Those votes can then be used to calculate an Elo-style score, often through approaches such as the Bradley–Terry model, giving users a simple way to understand how different systems perform based on human preference.

Human feedback remains an important part of evaluating speech quality, but relying only on arena-style voting can be difficult as new TTS models are released at a rapid pace. Open-source models can also face practical barriers because they generally need to be hosted and served by the evaluation platform, while API-based commercial models can be added more easily. This can result in open-weight systems being less visible on public leaderboards. Another challenge is consistency: people's preferences and listening criteria can change over time, meaning that votes collected months apart may not always represent exactly the same standards.

Open TTS Leaderboard aims to address these challenges by providing a scalable and transparent space for evaluating multilingual TTS and voice-cloning systems. The goal is to make comparisons easier to reproduce, expand coverage of open models, and provide useful evaluation signals alongside human preference. By bringing together scalable testing and community feedback, the project can help researchers, developers, and users better understand how speech models perform across different languages, voices, and use cases.

GitHub repo with the eval scripts is public! https://github.com/huggingface/open-tts-leaderboard

InfoQ Homepage News Cloudflare’s Post-Quantum GeoKey Manager Enters Closed Beta without Attribute-Based Encryption

Oct 31, 2026 3 min read

Cloudflare has moved a post-quantum rebuild of GeoKey Manager into closed beta, protecting geographically fenced decryption keys with a hybrid of ML-KEM-768 and X25519 and replacing the attribute-based encryption the service has relied on since 2022. The beta opened on October 23 to existing Data Localization Suite customers, with general availability planned for the first quarter of 2027.

Chetan Agrawal, Arka Nayan and Erik Engstrom describe the redesign as addressing two requirements at once: data sovereignty rules that confine plaintext processing to a region, and harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks in which traffic captured today is decrypted once a quantum computer exists. GeoKey Manager first shipped in 2017 for TLS keys and moved to ciphertext-policy attribute-based encryption in 2022. Cloudflare gives two reasons for dropping that scheme: no production-ready post-quantum variant exists, and customers don't need the large number of regions it was built to express.

In its place, key protection uses HPKE, the hybrid public-key encryption construction defined in RFC 9180, with a key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) combining ML-KEM-768 and X25519, HKDF-SHA-256 and AES-256-GCM. Two kinds of keys replace the policy expressions. Regional root keys are 256-bit symmetric secrets held one per region. Application-specific key pairs are derived from a root for a single service, such as Tunnel or Gateway, and a single epoch, Cloudflare's term for a key generation that rotation advances. The key-management service derives the application key pair and wraps customer private keys under its public component.

The two kinds of keys travel different paths: Quicksilver, Cloudflare's globally replicated key-value store, carries wrapped keys and metadata everywhere, while regional root keys move a separate path through the provisioning service, which stores them in Vault. Before an edge server receives a root key, it must clear three checks: TPM hardware identity verification, a lookup in Zinc, Cloudflare's server inventory, that maps the identity to a data center and location, and a decision by the provisioning service about which roots that server may hold.

Authorized servers then load regional root keys into the kernel keyring rather than onto disk. Because that memory is volatile, "a machine restart removes the keys," and the server has to authenticate again. Regional membership refreshes several times a day as the network changes, separately from key rotation and without customer action.

Dabeer Shaikh, a senior solutions engineer at HashiCorp, asked under Cloudflare's announcement how a geo-fenced key can be rotated without downtime, and the post answers that question through its epoch model. A soft rotation creates a new epoch while a limited number of previous epochs stay usable, so customers keep uptime during the transition; a hard rotation rewraps affected keys under a replacement epoch and removes access to the previous one.

Mark Tehrani, founder of CyberSeQ and a professor of cybersecurity, posted five questions on the same thread. Four concern the blast radius of a compromised regional root key, whether a compromised Zinc inventory or provisioning service could hand regional keys to an out-of-region server, what protects keys exposed before a rotation, and whether a compromised control plane could alter regional membership. The fifth goes to the design's central tradeoff:

If regional key provisioning, synchronization, or rotation fails, could the fail-closed design cause a region-wide service outage?

Cloudflare's post is explicit about that behavior. Any failed check on service context, region, or epoch rejects the request, and at the edge a missing or malformed key means the service does not start. The authors call failing closed "a very intentional design choice." The trust boundary covers the key-management, provisioning, and authorized edge key services; Quicksilver sits outside it because it only ever holds wrapped keys and metadata.

The rebuild extends a pattern in Cloudflare's post-quantum work. As previously reported on InfoQ, Cloudflare adopted hybrid ML-KEM for its IPsec service in March, when over 60% of human-generated TLS traffic on its network already used it, and the company has since set out plans for a quantum-safe certificate authority. Most regions will be covered at launch, with product-specific caveats. What the beta will show is whether the design's answer to a failed check, refusing to serve, is one customers accept at regional scale.
