#9874. Exposed to PHP2Shell? Cyber Experts Weigh in With Advice

Fixing the critical PHP flaws is not as simple as clicking "Update." Here's how to assess your risk, and what you can do to protect yourself.

New data shows that organizations aren't moving to patch PHP2Shell as fast as attackers are moving to exploit it. It's understandable, cybersecurity experts say, because updating in this case is especially complicated.

The data began trickling in on Oct. 21, painting a picture of the world's initial response to the new PHP vulnerabilities. The picture wasn't pretty.

Some well-positioned experts picked up on a remarkable volume of threat activity. Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince stated that in the 10 hours before the vulnerabilities were publicly disclosed on Oct. 21, his company observed thousands of exploitation attempts. "That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now," he wrote on X, late on Oct. 21.

The next day, Check Point Research claimed that attempts at exploitation had already reached 10% of organizations worldwide. On the flip side, only a small percentage of vulnerable organizations have been visibly updating to new PHP releases.

Related:Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks

Using discoverable deployments on Shodan as a sample, Ox Security researchers found that more than 99% of instances were not yet advertising a newly patched version 24 hours after fixed versions were made available. Researchers at Flare piled on, noting that 73% of those instances advertised PHP branches that no longer receive updates from the PHP Foundation. (It also qualified these figures, noting that basic Internet scanning misses some crucial nuances.)

Meanwhile, Cisco Talos estimated, based on open source intelligence (OSINT), that around half of all PHP systems won't receive patches.

On the morning of Oct. 23, Eastern time, Ox informed Dark Reading that its 99% figure had dropped to 97.5%. And Flare told Dark Reading that of the 27% of public records reflecting upstream-supported branches, about 5% have been updated.

Addressing PHP2Shell is often not as simple as clicking "Update," practitioners acknowledge. Still, there are steps that most organizations can take to protect themselves immediately, like diligently looking for PHP deployments across an organization's entire fleet of systems, hunting for signs of compromise, and restricting access to or otherwise taking offline any systems that can't be patched immediately.

In principle, protecting against PHP2Shell should be simple. There are new versions one can update to, which cover the vulnerabilities in question, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. In practice, addressing PHP2Shell will look very different from one organization to the next, and require more or less effort, depending on how, where, and in what ways they use PHP.

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

The unanimous first step all cybersecurity experts point to is that organizations should discover and inventory all of the assets they have running PHP. It's easier said than done. As the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) noted in an Oct. 21 security alert, PHP isn't just something that runs websites; it's "often a component of other software and prevalence may not be directly observable."

Flare researchers saw that firsthand when examining the attack surface. "What stood out to me during the research was how much PHP we found outside conventional web hosting," says Adrian Cheek, senior cybercrime researcher at Flare. "We identified it in storage devices, physical access-control systems, cameras and remote-access interfaces. If you're only looking at your main websites or limiting an external assessment to ports 80 and 443, you're going to miss some of that."

For organizations with this sort of exposure, he continues, "You generally can't log into a storage appliance or physical access-control unit and independently upgrade its PHP installation. You need the manufacturer to provide updated firmware. If the manufacturer has stopped supporting that product, the organization may have no patch available."

Related:GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

Putting edge cases aside, let's assume that an organization has managed to find and list out all of its PHP deployments. From there, remarkably, things only get more complicated.

Publicly available data seems to suggest that most PHP out in the world is running on old branches. "If you’re running an application built around PHP 5 or PHP 7, moving to a current PHP release could mean rewriting parts of the application, replacing dependencies, and testing everything that might break. There’s a good reason why organizations avoid doing that casually, particularly when the application supports something operationally important," Cheek explains.

In these cases, remediation will be a slow process, if organizations choose to pursue it at all. Luckily, and confusingly, old PHP versions aren't always unsavable.

The most common version in public records, 7.4.3, is what shipped with Ubuntu 20.04. As Cheek points out, "Linux distributions frequently retain an older PHP version number while backporting security fixes. So an old version number doesn't automatically mean the software hasn't been patched." Besides operating systems, applications can also backport fixes for the PHP they come packaged with.

Thus, organizations running outdated PHP actually fall into very distinct buckets: Some organizations will need to do the heavy lifting necessary to migrate or replace their applications or products. In the meantime, experts say, they should consider taking their vulnerable systems offline entirely. Cheek also offers one pro tip to mitigate CVE-2026-109619, for those that can reach the PHP configuration.

"The reported attacks run through PHP session upload progress, a feature that is on by default and needs no session_start call in the application. Disabling session.upload_progress.enabled and restarting the PHP workers blocks the confirmed session-upload-progress attack paths without requiring a PHP version upgrade," he explains, with the qualification that it doesn't address the other PHP2Shell flaw, CVE-2026-109618, so it's a temporary measure at best.

Some organizations will be privileged enough to install backported fixes through their vendors. On Oct. 21, Ubuntu developer Canonical published fixes for PHP2Shell for all versions since 14.04. Even these relieved parties will have more accounting work to do, since an OS or application update doesn't necessarily carry a full PHP version upgrade. If one takes advantage of Ubuntu's updates, future scans could continue to show it ostensibly running PHP 7.4.3.

And don't forget, Cheek says: "The restart matters. Installing a corrected PHP package doesn't necessarily replace the interpreter already loaded into running worker processes."

Besides all of the technical details, size will determine a lot about how organizations can respond to PHP2Shell.

As with any urgent cybersecurity vulnerability, small businesses may start off with disadvantages in awareness as well as the resources needed to get themselves cleaned up. Yet after 48 hours of working nonstop to help more than 1,000 organizations with PHP2Shell, OX Security CEO Neatsun Ziv is quicker to point out the advantages in being small. "

At small organizations, you can do whatever you want. You just go in and patch. You wait five hours. Nobody complains about breaking anything," he says.

But larger organizations are different, he says. "They've got a golden image — one server baseline they update," Ziv says. "It's always a downstream model: you deploy a new golden image, this golden image is then being built with new software, this new software goes to production, and nobody can change production. This is the norm in deployments today. Nobody goes to servers and actually patches them. It just becomes unmaintainable in the long term."

And that's to say nothing of just how many people from different teams need to be involved in major updates within a large organization; or of how major organizations run disproportionately significant systems that can't afford to break; or of how prevalent and varied PHP can be even within organizations. As Ziv notes, "Most of the organizations that we work with found hundreds of servers that are running PHP."

Check Point chief security and trust officer Alex Spokoiny adds that even beyond one's own house, organizations also face risk from how all of their suppliers handle PHP2Shell.

"The first step is to engage the relevant suppliers and understand how they are responding. Are they affected? What protections have they put in place? When do they expect remediation to be completed? If you cannot get clear or reasonable answers to those questions, that is itself something you need to factor into your risk assessment and potentially consider alternative options," he advises.

Organizations can also team up, to everyone's benefit. "For example, where technically possible, they may be able to extend their own Web application firewall (WAF) protection to applications operated by third parties, helping reduce exposure while the provider works toward a permanent fix," Spokoiny says.

Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9872. Trust Is Not What It Seems — and Fraudsters Are Counting on It

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Threat actors don't need to rely on malware to breach organizations anymore. They're simply calling help desks and politely asking for access, with a little help from artificial intelligence.

After a disruptive cyberattack hits, customer trust can take a while to rebuild. But now threat actors are impersonating trusted brand names and existing customer accounts to abuse customer relations.

"Trust has become easier to exploit and harder to establish," a new TransUnion report warns. Threat actors use social engineering, deepfake technology, text spoofing, compromised credentials, and artificial intelligence (AI) to become whoever they need to be, whether that's a new or existing customer or the organization itself.

In light of more attacks, many organizations have improved security during sign-up and onboarding processes. Organizations must continue to adapt since "most fraud now occurs after the customer relationship has already been established," the report states. It found 58% of organizations were very or extremely concerned that fraud is evolving faster than their abilities to detect or prevent it.

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

The use of synthetic identities plays a big role. Threat actors can spin them up with ease, given widespread data breaches that exposed millions of individuals' sensitive information, says Brian Killeen, vice president of global identity solutions at TransUnion. Scammers will replicate leaked documents or use deepfakes to bypass identity proofing checks at onboarding.

The credit reporting agency found that account login accounted for 53% of all suspected digital fraud during the first half of 2026. Conducting scams has become easier for threat actors as tooling advances, Killeen adds. Threat actors aren't just automating account creation with scripts; they're actually building logic into automated pipelines to reverse-engineer security controls, he says. That allows them to pinpoint exactly where and how defenses are blocking their attacks.

"Trust is under pressure," Killeen tells Dark Reading.

Last year the FBI warned of an uptick in cybercriminals targeting employee self-service portals — websites used for payroll, benefits, and other human resources services — at both private companies and government agencies. Threat actors created fake search engine advertisements to lure users into visiting malicious sites that mimicked legitimate companies' logos and layouts. Once the victim logged in, attackers stole login credentials and financial information.

And the situation continues to evolve. Over the past year, AI has helped criminals personalize attacks and spread them across channels — from email to Teams. Deepfakes add another layer of credibility, says Javvad Malik, lead chief information security officer (CISO) adviser at KnowBe4.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

Amid booming AI adoption that security has trouble matching, the security awareness company is also seeing more attempts to exploit AI systems or take advantage of poorly configured AI tools and agents, he adds.

"The social engineering techniques remain similar, but attackers are also using AI to find weaknesses and are beginning to target AI agents directly," Malik tells Dark Reading.

The AI attack surface is ripe for the taking. New research from Check Point on brand impersonation trends from Q3 flagged a phishing campaign where threat actors impersonated Anthropic's Claude assistant. Fraudulent emails, playing up urgency with a due payment notice, requested 500 euros with an "update payment" link intended to trick users into clicking, putting their credentials and financial information at risk. Since April, KnowBe4 tracked a 228% increase in AI brand impersonation, says James Dyer, head of threat intelligence. Attackers are abusing the global focus on using AI within businesses as a perfect covert operation for their phishing attacks, he adds, warning that the problem compounds when attackers center their attacks around breaking news headlines.

Related:As AI Risks Grow, Insurers Split on Covering the Damage

When it comes to attacks against customer relations, attackers' methods have evolved from deploying malware to exploiting identity because there's no need to write a script when they can just get a password reset, says Dave Lewis, global advisory CISO at 1Password.

The industry spent a decade training people not to click links, and attackers responded by simply asking nicely, he adds. The most common attacks he has observed don't involve "anyone in a hoodie typing furiously" but instead phoning the help desk to manipulate users into giving away multifactor authentication (MFA) codes.

"[It's] the most effective zero-day of 2026," Lewis says.

Walking in through the customer relationship management (CRM) system's front door is another tactic he has seen, pointing to the data-theft campaign against Salesforce customers that started in 2025 and continued into 2026.

"Nobody 'hacks' the CRM," Lewis tells Dark Reading. "They just log in with a key you handed to a vendor or a guest account nobody remembers creating."

The target moved from the data center to the software-as-a-service layer, where one compromised integration gives attackers many targets per compromise. Detection lags because SaaS platforms log differently from traditional infrastructure, Lewis adds.

Threat actors also use AI to build voice deepfakes from executives' public recordings, deploy them in high-pressure desk calls, and then use AI again to move through hybrid environments within minutes of gaining access. But that doesn't exactly signal an increase in sophistication, Lewis says.

"Technical sophistication is down," he says. "Operational sophistication — research, patience, scripting, follow-through — is up. It's less of the 'evil genius' and more 'well-run call center with bad intentions.'"

"What once looked legitimate and trusted can change" as threat actors slip further under the radar, cloaked behind more convincing and personalized impersonation tactics. Killeen stresses. Organizations across industries are seeing more scams, authorized fraud, and good customers being manipulated, he says.

Organizations must learn and adapt quickly because attackers aren't wasting any time. Killeen recommends that organizations take a look at their existing controls to uncover vulnerable points and understand where the biggest losses are. Even if organizations stand up strong security at the front door, they could still fall victim to downstream risks.

"It's taking a risk-based approach, looking at things holistically, and how you prioritize those things accordingly, based on your vulnerabilities," Killeen advises.

Killeen and Lewis agree that attacks against customer relations warrants checking every door leading into the CRM. That includes every OAuth application, integration, guest or portal user, and API key.

"Revoke anything without a named owner," Lewis says. "Scope the rest. Repeat quarterly because they grow back."

He also recommends that organizations fix the help desk process attackers continually abuse, rather than people who work it. Scripted identity verification for resets, callback to a number of record, and manager approval for any privileged or MFA reset are ways to reduce risk in that area.

"Drop speed metrics, like average handle time, for identity-sensitive support interactions," Lewis adds. “They drive agents to prioritize speed over verification.”

Holding less customer data is another area organizations can prioritize to limit risks. Implement retention limits on customer records, purge dormant accounts, and don't include production customer data in sandboxes, Lewis recommends.

"Data you don't hold can't be stolen," he says.

Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

NetBSD is a free, fast, secure, and highly portable Unix-like Open Source operating system. It is available for a wide range of platforms, from large-scale servers and powerful desktop systems to handheld and embedded devices. Its clean design and advanced features make it excellent for use in both production and research environments, and the source code is freely available under a business-friendly license. NetBSD is developed and supported by a large and vibrant international community. Many applications are readily available through pkgsrc, the NetBSD Packages Collection.

The NetBSD Foundation was chartered in 1995, with the task of overseeing core NetBSD project services, promoting the project within industry and the open source community, and holding intellectual property rights on much of the NetBSD code base. Day-to-day operations of the project are handled by volunteers.

#9870. AutoSynthData: Generating Training Data for Enterprise Agents

Enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments. The work they ask these agents to do is shaped by the systems they use, the rules they follow, and the state of their data. A model may be broadly capable and still struggle with a particular environment: a workflow it handles poorly, a combination of tools it misuses, or a constraint it fails to respect. Those are the weaknesses an enterprise needs to improve.

The difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data. An individual failure tells us something, but training a model requires many new tasks that exercise the same capability in different situations. Those tasks must also be possible to complete in the environment, resemble work someone would actually request, and have a reliable way to check whether the agent succeeded.

At ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data. It uses a target model’s failures and a stronger teacher’s successes to decide what the model should learn next, then generates and validates new tasks that exercise those capabilities. As the model improves, the curriculum shifts toward what it still finds difficult. We illustrate the pipeline with EnterpriseOps Gym (Malay et al., 2026), using the released dataset. We begin by describing the environment an agent operates in and what makes a task useful for training.

An agentic environment defines the world in which an agent operates: the state it can observe and modify, the tools and APIs it can invoke, and the state transitions produced by its actions.

A task is instantiated within this environment. We use the following abstraction:

The system specification defines the constraints under which the agent operates, including system instructions, environment policies, and, when applicable, task-specific initialization such as a seeded database state or a set of knowledge articles.

The specification must be compatible with the environment’s tools, state, and supported actions. Its instructions should be clear and avoid arbitrary constraints introduced solely to manufacture difficulty.

The user prompt specifies what the user wants the agent to accomplish, together with any user-level constraints. A generated task should satisfy three properties.

Feasibility. There should exist at least one trajectory in the current environment that satisfies the user prompt while respecting the system specification. This rules out tasks that depend on unavailable tools, inaccessible knowledge, impossible state transitions, or actions prohibited by policy.

Realism. The user prompt should resemble something a user would plausibly ask in the target environment. The space of executable behaviors is usually much larger than the space of realistic workflows.

Difficulty. For training, the task should expose a weakness of the current agent. Tasks that are already solved reliably provide little new training signal. The useful region is therefore tasks that are feasible and realistic, but not yet consistently solved.

The verifier determines whether the resulting trajectory successfully completes the task. It should satisfy three properties.

Consistency. It should agree with the user prompt, the system specification, and the task-specific environment state.

Soundness. It should reject trajectories that fail to satisfy the task or violate relevant constraints.

Completeness. It should accept valid solutions rather than encode one particular reference trajectory.

These properties matter directly during training. A lax verifier can reward incorrect behavior, while an overly restrictive verifier can penalize valid solutions.

Given an environment and a target model, AutoSynthData generates training tasks consisting of a system specification, user prompt, and verifier. The generated tasks are grounded in the environment and selected to provide useful training signal for the current model.

AutoSynthData first evaluates the target model in the environment using diagnostic tasks and identifies patterns in the tasks it struggles to complete. A stronger teacher helps characterize which of those tasks are solvable and what successful behavior looks like. AutoSynthData turns the resulting capability gaps into new executable tasks, checks each task in the environment, and uses accepted samples for post-training. Evaluating the updated model reveals which gaps remain and can guide the next round of generation.

AutoSynthData uses evaluation runs in the target environment to identify what the model needs to learn next. In our EnterpriseOps Gym experiment, we run both the target model and a stronger teacher on the evaluation tasks. We examine those runs to identify:

We distill these findings into sanitized capability specification cards. The evaluation tasks guide what the model should learn, but the generator does not receive their original prompts, entities, trajectories, or verifier details. It receives the cards and uses them to create new tasks with different prompts, states, and solution paths.

Identifying a capability gap tells us what to teach, but training requires many varied tasks that exercise it. AutoSynthData uses the specification card to generate those tasks.

Suppose the target model struggles with tasks that require the following workflow:

The generator creates new tasks that exercise this workflow, varying the entities, initial environment state, workflow composition, tool combinations, wording, and difficulty. The stronger teacher then demonstrates a successful trajectory for each task. For supervised fine-tuning (SFT), these demonstrations teach the target model how to apply the capability in new situations.

AutoSynthData builds the dataset in two phases: first generating and validating core samples, then expanding them into novel variants.

The target phase creates the core set of training samples from the capability specifications. Workers generate independent tasks in parallel, picking up a new target when they finish. Each candidate goes through validation, execution, solver evaluation, and repair before acceptance. The result is a batch of vetted examples built around what the target model needs to learn.

The multiply phase expands the dataset by creating novel variants of accepted target samples. Each variant has its own user request, environment state, entity configuration, reference trajectory, and verifier, and must pass the same validation and execution checks. A multiplied sample cannot seed another multiplied sample. This anchors expansion to the vetted target set and limits drift across generations.

To support both phases, AutoSynthData separates generation control from environment-specific execution. A shared controller coordinates generation, quality control, coverage, and dataset construction, while an adapter handles environment execution, task and state management, reference replay, deterministic verification, solver execution, and task profiling.

Together, parallel target generation and multiplication provide a path to training-scale datasets. Their usefulness depends on the checks applied to every candidate: the task must be executable, the solution must work, and the verifier must distinguish success from failure.

Generating a plausible request is not enough to produce useful training data. A task may be impossible in the target environment, its reference solution may fail when executed, or its verifier may reward the wrong final state. AutoSynthData checks these properties before accepting a task for training.

AutoSynthData reviews quality at two levels: individual candidates must pass verification, and batches must provide useful coverage and diversity.

Each candidate must clear a quality-control loop before entering the training dataset. We begin with solver evaluation to measure difficulty. In the configuration used here, we favor tasks the target model solves on no more than one of three trials and the stronger solver solves on at least two of three trials. Candidates also undergo positive and negative verification and a bounded repair process.

The positive gate asks: Does the intended solution solve the generated task?

The pipeline executes the reference trajectory in the target environment and checks the resulting state against the candidate’s verifier. This reveals mismatches among the prompt, initial state, solution, and success criteria.

The negative gate asks: Do relevant incorrect outcomes fail?

For example, it can mutate parts of the expected outcome and confirm that those states no longer pass verification. This catches weak verifiers that award success without requiring the intended behavior.

Failed candidates go to a critic before being discarded. The critic examines the sample and its failure, looking for inconsistent state, impossible workflows, incorrect task construction, bad reference trajectories, weak verifier logic, or a mismatch with the intended capability. The critic’s findings guide repairs, with a fixed limit on retries:

A repaired task must pass the relevant checks again. The diagnosis guides repairs to the existing candidate rather than requiring generation to start over.

Passing these checks makes a sample eligible for training, but individually valid samples can still form a repetitive or unbalanced dataset. AutoSynthData therefore also reviews generation at the batch level.

A batch may overrepresent a few easy task families, miss a capability, or reflect too much generation effort spent on a low-yield pattern.

A meta-review examines accepted samples, rejected samples, and generation behavior across each batch. It asks:

The controller tracks coverage in the accepted dataset, reduces generation in overrepresented regions, and directs more work toward gaps. When a region repeatedly produces poor candidates, critiques and meta-review guide changes to the generation strategy. These adjustments balance useful learning signal, task quality, coverage, diversity, and low redundancy within the available generation budget and dataset size requirements.

Together, these feedback loops improve both individual tasks and the dataset they form: sample-level checks guide candidate repair, while batch-level review guides future generation.

The useful training distribution changes as the model improves. AutoSynthData treats synthetic data generation as a search for tasks near the target model's capability boundary: difficult enough to expose weaknesses, but solvable enough for the teacher to provide reliable demonstrations.

After post-training, we evaluate the updated model in the same environment. Tasks it now solves reliably are less useful for the next training round; persistent failures point to capabilities that still need attention. Those results can guide the next generation round.

Our experiments focus on SFT, but the same mechanism could support reinforcement learning (RL): generate tasks that challenge the current policy and provide reliable learning signal, train, then move the generation target with the updated policy. We plan to test this moving, difficulty-calibrated frontier beyond SFT.

We use EnterpriseOps Gym to test whether this approach improves a model on tasks in a stateful enterprise environment. We generate training tasks in the Gym’s Hybrid and ITSM environments, fine-tune the target model on accepted samples, and evaluate the resulting checkpoints.

We tested the pipeline on the Hybrid domain of EnterpriseOps Gym using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and Qwen3.8-27B as the teacher.

AutoSynthData generated 2,000 synthetic training samples in about 18 hours. We fine-tuned Gemma on this dataset and evaluated the resulting checkpoints on the benchmark. The best checkpoint was epoch 5.

The synthetic SFT checkpoint improves mean Pass@1 by 7.2 percentage points, a 35% relative improvement, and raises verifier success from 63.01% to 68.55%. It closes 59% of the original Pass@1 gap between Gemma and the reference model.

The training tasks were newly generated from capability specifications; the generator did not receive the original evaluation tasks. The result demonstrates improvement in EnterpriseOps Gym Hybrid, the environment used for this experiment.

We also applied AutoSynthData to the ITSM domain of EnterpriseOps Gym, using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as the teacher. AutoSynthData generated 1,994 synthetic training samples in 66 hours. Generation took longer than in the subsequent Hybrid run described above, primarily because the ITSM run used a larger teacher model and preceded pipeline optimizations that improved throughput.

On ITSM, synthetic SFT raises mean Pass@1 from 18.77% to 27.18%, showing that the approach also improves performance in a second domain.

The tasks most useful for training depend on both the environment and the model working in it. AutoSynthData uses the model’s failures to choose what to generate, validates new tasks against the environment, and makes those tasks available for post-training. Our EnterpriseOps Gym results show the value of that approach in a controlled setting. As the model changes, the same process can focus on the gaps that remain.

InfoQ Homepage News File Mover Express: AWS Releases Open-Source Tool for S3 File Transfers

Nov 01, 2026 2 min read

AWS has recently released File Mover Express, an open-source application under the Apache 2.0 license for transferring large files between local systems and Amazon S3. Available for macOS, Windows, and Linux, it supports parallel transfers, automatic performance tuning, retries, pause and resume, and file integrity verification.

Designed to "move media to S3 at wire speed," File Mover Express supports auto-tuned parallel transfers, pause and resume, a desktop GUI, a scriptable CLI, and automatic uploads from monitored folders.

The project is primarily developed in Go for its transfer engine and TypeScript with Angular for its graphical interface. It also supports integration with AI assistants through MCP and OIDC-based authentication with identity providers. Provanshu Dey, senior solutions architect at AWS, Asbjorn Kjaer, senior software engineer at AWS, Matthew Muccio, solutions architect at AWS, and Ross Dickson, senior customer solutions manager at AWS, explain:

At the core of File Mover Express is a daemon-based transfer engine that decouples transfers from your desktop session. The daemon can run on the machine of your choice, whether that is your workstation, a server in the data center, or an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance, while you control it from a drag-and-drop graphical user interface (GUI) or a scriptable command line interface (CLI) over an encrypted, password-protected connection.

Media teams regularly transfer terabytes of assets between on-premises storage and the cloud. These transfers often involve tight deadlines and processes that must continue after the initiating user or machine disconnects. Traditional transfer clients may stop when a desktop session ends, while commercial alternatives can introduce licensing costs, proprietary protocols, or third-party infrastructure. File Mover Express supports uploads and downloads, allowing teams to transfer large files to Amazon S3 and retrieve them for editing, review, or restoration.

File Mover Express splits large files into chunks and uploads them in parallel using multipart uploads. With the autotuning mode, it adjusts the number of parallel streams and chunk sizes to optimize throughput for the available connection. Transfers also support configurable retries and file-level pause and resume. Dey, Kjaer, Muccio, and Dickson add:

File Mover Express provides security features including file encryption in flight, file encryption at rest, and encryption for the control plane. All transfers use HTTPS, and access to your S3 buckets is governed by AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) with a documented minimum-permission policy (...) For teams that centralize identity, File Mover Express supports single sign-on through OpenID Connect (OIDC).

File Mover Express calculates checksums in the background and caches them locally for reuse when files remain unchanged. It supports MD5, XXHash, XXHash64, and XXH3, offering a choice between compatibility and hashing performance. For transfers to distant buckets, users can enable S3 Transfer Acceleration, while bandwidth limits help control network usage. On LinkedIn, Dickson writes:

Moving large media files to the cloud shouldn't be the slow part of your day :) That’s why a group of us at AWS built File Mover Express (...) For anyone in media moving camera cards, dailies, or deliverables, it tackles the usual pain.

The project's source code is available on GitHub, along with pre-built packages for macOS, Windows, and Linux.

#9868. Shutting the Door on the XCPE Botnet (Threat Intelligence)

Last week, Google and industry partners dismantled the XCPE backdoor which enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet. We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology Co., an Android Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) and Original Device Manufacturer (ODM). Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates' malware modules onto infected devices. These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices. #9867. 10 Software Security Practices Built for the Next 250 Years

This Cybersecurity Awareness Month's theme, "Securing the Next 250," asks us to look beyond vulnerabilities and consider what will make our digital systems resilient for generations.

When I testified before Congress with my L0pht colleagues in 1998, we warned that insecure software could put the systems society depended on at risk. Technology has changed dramatically since then, but the fundamental security questions remain familiar. Where does untrusted data enter? What authority does a component have? Who owns the risk, and how do we know a control worked?

We cannot predict the technology stack of 2276, but we can establish practices that make software trustworthy as technology evolves. These 10 are a good place to start.

Make security part of the architecture. Secure by design should describe how a system is engineered, beginning with secure defaults, approved patterns, clear trust boundaries, and controls that make insecure outcomes difficult. When security is introduced near the end of development, it must work against decisions already embedded in the architecture, while built-in controls become part of how the system operates and evolves.

Maintain an accurate picture of what you have. Every organization needs a continuously updated inventory of its applications, open source dependencies, development tools, AI models, and external services, along with clear ownership for critical systems. When a serious vulnerability emerges, teams should be able to determine quickly where the affected component is running, what it can reach, and who is responsible for addressing it.

Verify every line of code. Code should earn trust whether it was written by an employee, generated by an AI assistant, or obtained from a third party. Our research found that 44% of AI-generated coding tasks introduced a known vulnerability, which means organizations adopting these tools need independent security testing that operates at the same speed as development and verifies code before it reaches production.

Make the secure path the easiest path. Developers work under constant pressure to ship, so security controls that produce excessive noise, delay builds, or pull people away from their normal tools will eventually be bypassed. Organizations should put precise feedback, approved components, and validated fixes directly into repositories, pipelines, and coding workflows, making the secure approach the most efficient way to complete the work.

Match security speed to development speed. AI is turning software insecurity into a throughput problem because teams can now produce and change code faster than manual review can follow. Testing, policy enforcement, and remediation therefore need to operate continuously across the development life cycle, with automation handling repeatable work and people concentrating on the complex decisions that require business context and judgment.

Control what enters the software supply chain. Modern applications are assembled from large volumes of code that organizations did not write, and each dependency introduces another relationship that must be understood and maintained. Teams should evaluate components when they enter a build, record their provenance, detect malicious or abandoned packages, and plan for safe upgrades, since an inventory alone cannot prevent risky software from being introduced.

Pay down security debt before it comes due. Veracode's research found that security debt now affects 82% of organizations, leaving an expanding reservoir of vulnerabilities that have remained unresolved for more than a year. As AI-powered discovery compresses years of vulnerability research into months, leaders need to fund remediation as an ongoing engineering function, define expectations for addressing the highest-risk flaws, and track whether new risk is accumulating faster than teams can remove it.

Measure the risk you remove. Most security programs can report how many vulnerabilities they found and closed, yet those activity measures do not show whether the organization has become safer. More useful measures include how long critical, exploitable flaws remain exposed, whether fix capacity is keeping pace with incoming risk and how quickly teams can reduce exposure in applications tied to sensitive data or essential business operations.

Threat-model the entire AI system. An AI agent includes far more than the model because its identity, permissions, tools, memory, data, runtime, and network access all contribute to what it can ultimately do. Organizations should authorize sensitive actions where they occur, constrain what compromised components can reach, include the runtime in data-flow analysis, and retain enough evidence to determine what the agent did when something goes wrong.

Preserve human accountability. Every important application and accepted risk needs an accountable owner, supported by evidence of the controls applied, tests performed, and decisions made throughout the software life cycle. As machines assume a larger role in writing and modifying code, people must retain enough understanding to challenge the output, recognize unexpected behavior, and demonstrate that reasonable precautions were taken.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

The next 250 years will bring technologies that we cannot name today, although the systems built with them will still have inputs, privileges, dependencies, and consequences. Lasting security will come from disciplined engineering, continuous verification, and clear responsibility, supported by people who understand how complex systems fail and know how to question the assumptions behind them.

Related:Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

That hacker mindset has served the industry well, and we need to keep teaching it to developers, defenders, and the next generation of security researchers. The tools and architectures will continue to change, while our responsibility to build systems worthy of trust will endure.

Related:PapRAT Cyber-Espionage Campaign Leaves a 'Bitter' Taste in South Asia

Founder and Chief Security Evangelist, Veracode

Chris Wysopal is the Chief Security Evangelist at Veracode, responsible for enhancing the company’s industry presence, advocating robust security practices, and fostering customer and peer relationships. Prior to co-founding Veracode in 2006, Chris was vice president of research and development at security consultancy @stake, which was acquired by Symantec. In the 1990s, Chris was one of the original vulnerability researchers at The L0pht, a hacker think tank, where he was one of the first to publicize the risks of insecure software. He has testified to the US Congress on the subjects of government security and how vulnerabilities are discovered in software.

#9866. The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

Microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row. It is now available through Hugging Face.

Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper.

A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.

The AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation.

Then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ”

Two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold, pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked.

An AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees.

That gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv.

You can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006, and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper.

Want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself.

Final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question.

The gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap.

A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.

An agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times, each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things:

Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers.

We use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing.

Starting with the familiar view. The table below reports pass@1, the single-attempt score estimate, broken out by domain. This is the number most leaderboards publish, and on its own it reads like an ordinary capability ranking.

Table 2: ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain. Each model is evaluated on every task for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the group leader; underline marks the runner-up. The standard errors for the single attempt score estimates are provided in Table 4 in our ThinkingBox paper.

Claude Opus 5.5 leads overall at 67.16%, two-thirds of a point above Claude Opus 5. Kimi-K3 is the strongest open-weights model, within a point of GPT-6-Astra. Domain matters just as much: Claude Opus 4.6 scores 68.62% on retail but 8.30% on auto insurance.

One good run tells you a model can do the work. It does not tell you whether it will do it again. So run every task 20 times and ask how much of that score survives.

Figure 2: How much of each model's single-attempt score survives 20 repeats.

Only three hold on to most of their pass@1 scores: GPT-6 Astra retains 78% of its single-attempt rate, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 each retain 71%. At the other end, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro each keep about 8%.

The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story.

Figure 3: Breadth and consistency pull apart. Twelve of the eighteen models are shown; six below 33% pass@1 are omitted for legibility.

Kimi-K3 has the broadest coverage of any model we tested. It solves 93.89% of the benchmark at least once: 476 of 507 tasks. Only 31 tasks defeat it entirely, the lowest count in the field. On retail workflows it leads outright at 82.24% pass@1, ahead of every proprietary model.

Kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts.

Claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt.

A newer model does not fix this. Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than Claude Opus 5 on every-attempt average, 67.16% against 66.50%, and solves more tasks at least once. It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches real records, pass@20 is the wrong column to look at.

Capability comparisons usually stop at the score. For anyone deploying, the relevant question is what a successful unit of work costs. We measure that as cost per successful task attempt. We say task attempt because every benchmark task is run repeatedly and cost is incurred per attempt, so pass@1 is the matching quality denominator.

We took each model's recorded token usage from its full 507 × 20 campaign and priced it at undiscounted list rates available on OpenRouter+, reversing promotional discounts and excluding endpoints that declare quantization. Input, output and cache rates all come from one provider endpoint per model.

Then we divided one run's cost by the number of attempts that succeeded:

Cost per successful task attempt = estimated cost for 507 attempts, one per task ÷ (507 × pass@1)

This is a comparative efficiency index, not an invoice, and not the price of serving one production request. It also prices single successes, not consistency. We price consistency next.

Example: GPT-5.4 costs $43.49 for 507 attempts (one attempt per task) and has 65.36% pass@1, so $43.49 ÷ (507 × 0.6536) = $0.131 per successful task attempt.

A model is on the frontier if no other model is both no more expensive and at least as accurate. Three models qualify; every other model is dominated on at least one axis.

Figure 4: Cost per successful task attempt against pass@1. Ringed dots are pareto cost frontier models.

The frontier has three steps. GPT-5.6 Sol has the lowest cost per success at $0.127; GPT-5.4 raises pass@1 by 3.45 percentage points for $0.004 more per success; Claude Opus 5.5 adds another 1.80 points at $0.276 per success. Each of the three remains on the cost frontier line because no cheaper model matches its pass@1.

Claude Opus 5 is the clearest case: at $0.475 per successful attempt and 66.50% pass@1, it is both more expensive and less accurate than Claude Opus 5.5 at $0.276 and 67.16%.

Cost per success rewards a model that is cheap and often right. It does not reward a model that is right every time. So we also compute cost per dependable task: the cost of the full 20-run campaign divided by the number of tasks the model passed on all 20 attempts.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of 20 runs of 507 attempts ÷ tasks passing 20/20

Example: GPT-6-Astra costs 20 × $86.03 = $1,720.60 for the campaign and passes 231 tasks on every attempt, so $1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $7.45 per dependable task.

Table 3: The nine lowest costs per dependable task among models with at least one observed 20/20 task, sorted low to high. Estimated $, not actual cloud bills.

Now rank by consistency. GPT-5.4 is the cheapest at $6.80, though only 128 tasks meet the bar. GPT-6 Astra reaches 231 at $7.45, and Claude Opus 5.5 the joint-highest 241 at $7.80.

None of the three dominates the others: each additional dependable task costs more. Claude Opus 5 also passes 241, but at $13.30, so Opus 5.5 dominates it outright. GPT-5.6 Sol, the cheapest per single success at $0.127, costs $9.76 per dependable task. The cheapest way to get a right answer is not the cheapest way to get a dependable one.

We assign each failed trace one deterministic diagnostic signature, and the headline is actionable: roughly four in five failures are tool handling, not reasoning. Across an ablation study in Table 5 of our paper:

These are unweighted averages of per-model shares and observable labels, not unique causal explanations.

The practical pattern is simple: agents usually get far enough to attempt the workflow, then fail to recover from tool errors, failed preconditions, or empty lookups. That is a retry and error-recovery problem before it is a model problem.

Difficulty also changes by domain: across the models listed in Table 2 above, retail averages 59.52% pass@1 while auto insurance averages 33.83%.

What to do about it. Treat the 20/20 rate as a design input, not a verdict. The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it.

Classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. We have not measured the lift from any of these on this benchmark, which is exactly the kind of thing the environment now makes testable.

ThinkingBox is the agent sandbox, while ThinkingBox-Bench is a dataset benchmark to evaluate agents. The diagram at the top of this post shows the loop; here is what each part does.

Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges.

Each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked.

Every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful.

At the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects. For requirements with no clean database value ("did the agent disclose this is not guaranteed?"), a narrow binary rubric question handles the semantics. 477 of the 507 tasks are graded on state alone; 30 add response rubrics.

The trust boundary: the model sees tasks, dialogue and tool schemas. Golden state, assertions, grading internals and credentials stay on the evaluator side.

ThinkingBox is now on Hugging Face, both the harness and the dataset. ThinkingBox-Bench now sits behind the OpenEnv interface, and each finished episode returns a binary pass/fail reward. The released adapter is designed for evaluation; separate, non-benchmark scenarios can use the same interface in training workflows.

Tested on Linux and WSL, with Python 3.11+, uv and Docker. You also need a thinkingbox-data checkout at the pinned release and model endpoints for the agent, simulated user and judge. One endpoint can serve all three roles, which is the simplest way to start. The OpenEnv image starts only the OpenEnv API; everything else you run yourself.

In a second terminal, start Typesense 30.1 and wait for its health check:

In a third terminal, start the Session Proxy and MCP servers.

Back in the first terminal, start the OpenEnv server against a ThinkingBox YAML config naming your three models (config guide):

Gate on readiness before running anything. It returns 503 until its observable data, configuration and Session Proxy checks pass. It cannot observe Typesense or live-probe every model endpoint, so confirm those separately:

Now score a real episode. example_usage.py only resets and lists tools; for agent actions, effects and assertions use the packaged evaluator:

The OpenEnv adapter writes operational failures to an errors sidecar so they can be rerun rather than silently mixed with model outcomes. A canonical result must resolve or explicitly account for those attempts; we counted system errors as unsuccessful trials.

Runs are gated on a pinned framework commit, a pinned data release and a bundle hash, so a canonical result is verifiable rather than asserted.

The useful part of this work is not our pass@1 leaderboard. It is the environment.

If you are evaluating an agent that touches real records:

Further details can be found in the following links:

ThinkingBox code is MIT-licensed; the benchmark data is CDLA-Permissive-2.0; the OpenEnv environment ships under OpenEnv's BSD-3-Clause.

Disclaimer: every task in the public benchmark is a synthetic reconstruction. The workflows and policies are modeled on real AI agentic enterprise patterns; the customers are not real.

ThinkingBox and ThinkingBox-Bench is built by the Microsoft Copilot Studio team in partnership with Toloka with collaborators from the University of Pittsburgh, Northwestern University, Columbia University and UC Irvine who interned at Microsoft. Questions are welcome in the comments section below or on github or by email at firstnamelastname@microsoft.com.

+ OpenRouter cost snapshot taken on Sept 20th 2026; Opus 5.5 pricing as per the Anthropic site.

ST003_006 delegates its pass check to validate_database. Unequal result and golden database hashes fail even when diff is empty. The diff explains a failure; it does not decide the pass.

This small replay exercises the released function with four authored effect inputs. Run python3 reproduce.py. It verifies the source pin and tests supplied hashes; it does not calculate a database hash, run an agent, or reproduce the full environment.

AI-assisted source reading and example by CyberNative AI LLC.

The useful cut is agent-reported "done" versus backend terminal state.

A green success from the same process that acted is a claim, not a grade. I'd want the eval to score durable side effects (ticket status, refund state, policy-cited fields) against a frozen oracle — and fail when the narrative is green while the database disagrees.

Practical check: can a run be marked done when the terminal-state fixture is red?

#9865. Observations from Running stealmybitcoin.com

Last week, I saw an article on the front page of the New York Times website reporting that a critical vulnerability in PHP had been found. The article, and others like it, claimed any attacker could achieve arbitrary remote code execution on any of the millions of running PHP services worldwide simply by sending a few unauthenticated web requests that exploited the PHP2Shell vulnerability.

My office Slack was buzzing, as were several of my Signal chats with colleagues and friends across the security community.

Rumors swirled about how in-the-wild exploitation caused one tech company to break embargo and leak news of the vulnerability hours before the rest of the community could coordinate disclosure. That hackers were already hacking websites, in the wild, with this exploit and that every hour mattered to get the patches rolled out across 70% of the internet.

Was PHP2Shell the hallmark of a new era whereby uplifted randos could hack any website with a few well-crafted prompts to an AI model?

I looked out my window, expecting perhaps to see the dull apocalyptic glow of fires on the horizon as society collapsed in real time. Nothing.

While online articles and tweets made the rounds about the eleven alarm cyberapocalypse upon us, I struggled to find any reference to a specific website that had been hacked.

Over the following days, a few iconoclasts had pointed out that the vulnerability was rather fiddly in practice (Elias Taylor; Lucas Luitjes) and that hacker groups, while initially quite excited by the exploit’s potential, had started to view it as impractical or difficult (KELA).

Yet at the same time, the national and international press continued to cover a herculean emergency effort to hunt down and patch PHP-based websites across the internet.

Rather than wait around and wonder, I decided to try to figure things out for myself. I had two fundamental questions:

Directly, the answers to the questions are:

Yes. Absolutely. The challenge winner, who has posted a writeup, exploited my server directly over an open internet connection and did so using the PHP2Shell vulnerability (e.g. he did not exploit some other vulnerability in my setup). He did this through a specially crafted exploit which targeted the specific configuration of my PHP installation and the ways in which it was set up on the server.

Not yet. Of tens of thousands of people who attempted the exploit - including in a 9 hour period when the challenge was active after the first successful solve (more on that below…) - only two managed to trigger the print-flag binary and only one, the winner of the challenge, managed to do so in such a way as to extract useful content from the application.

The core idea was pretty simple. I’d rent a cheap VPS for a few weeks, slap a PHP website on it along with the key to a bitcoin wallet, and then wait and see if anyone managed to drain the wallet. Miraculously, the domain name “stealmybitcoin.com” was available, so I took this as a sign from the fates themselves that this experiment had the mandate of heaven.

I slapped $500 of bitcoin into a clean wallet, rented a $2.50/month Debian VPS from a web hosting provider, and told Codex to make me a basic webpage and stick it on the internet with PHP. I configured the server such that a single executable binary print-flag had permissions to read a flag file containing the WIF, took down my firewall, and posted the link to Hacker News to see if anyone would give the challenge a shot.

Things got a little crazy from there. Within the first hour of posting, the link had climbed to the front page of Hacker News (where it stayed for essentially an entire day) and my $2.50/month VPS was under so much load I couldn’t maintain an SSH session.

I eventually scaled my VPS up from 1 vCPU, 500 MB RAM and 10GB of disk space all the way to 2 vCPU, 4096 MB RAM, and 80 GB of SSD. Over the course of the challenge my VPS host temporarily took my site down once because they suspected it was subject to a Distributed Denial of Service attack and once because “we have determined your CPU resource utilization profile is excessive.”

Additionally, due to the nature of the exploit, people were pretty continuously taking down individual PHP workers from high request load, partially successful memory exploitation attempts, and general shenanigans.

Eventually I managed to get things into a relatively steady state (e.g. most people could connect to the website most of the time), with regular resets and health checks standing in for true high-availability hosting. Once the link dropped off the front page of Hacker News, traffic quieted down quite a bit as well.

Due to flaky monitoring, it’s hard to get representative statistics regarding visitor count and traffic patterns. I had set up some pretty reliable logging so I could know if/when the print-flag binary was called and some best-effort logging of web request headers and payloads so I could hopefully understand what happened around that time; for the first few hours of virality, I was blowing through my logrotate configuration (for ~80MB of storage) roughly every 4 minutes thanks to the attention on the site.

As a result, logs of certain PHP crashes and activity around the print-flag file were essentially complete over the duration of the challenge. Broader web request logging only covered 600-ish of the challenge’s 1,600-ish minute duration.

During the 10 hours when I had reliable web request logging:

There’s no statistically credible way to extrapolate over the missing netflow data, but I can confidently say that tens of thousands of players attempted to steal my bitcoin.

I had much more reliable logs of PHP server errors and print-flag executions since they were not rotated under heavy load and were relatively low volume. In these logs, over 26-ish hours, I observed:

My original expectation is that this would be a low traffic honeypot. A few people would poke at it on Hacker News and then it would eventually get snagged by some botnet/scanner/automated exploitation tool that would steal my bitcoin. I’d write a little blog post about the logs from the hour or so around the exploit and then move on.

I didn’t remotely expect it to go viral in the way that it did. The virality was nice - it brought a lot of eyes on the challenge, got me a quick answer to my research question, and some people even chipped in and increased the size of the bitcoin prize wallet.

The virality was also rough in that suddenly many actual PHP security experts (and many non-experts too) had opinions about me, my motivations, and my web administration skills!

The first critique was that the server was unexploitable. Some claimed that it was literally just an nginx page (e.g. no PHP at all), while others claimed that the specific configuration of the server made it impossible to exploit.

I’m still not 100% sure how correct these claims were, as some people were causing SIGSEGVs to throw on the original version of the challenge.

However, I did make several modifications to the website that I felt were fair adjustments to increase the feasibility of the challenge without just deliberately making the server vulnerable.

First, I added a php-version.php page, which was served alongside the already PHP-hosted index.html page, in case the active participation of the PHP interpreter was necessary for the exploit. While some of the early reporting on PHP2Shell suggested this maybe wasn’t a strict requirement of exploitation (e.g. https://www.wiz.io/blog/php2shell-php-rce : “Exploitation does not depend on a flaw in the application’s code: even a simple “Hello World” application running on an affected PHP version can be vulnerable.”), it seems plausible to me that the part of the PHP SAPI server that serves .html files could be immune to these tasks.

I also added a ping.php page that responds with the word pong whenever someone POSTS the value ping to the server. This very simple application was added in case exploitation required PHP to dynamically react to user-supplied input. To me these two requirements (reacts to user-supplied input, runs .php pages) are pretty universal across real-world applications, so adding support for these code paths did not undermine the spirit of the challenge.

There was some other feedback, which I largely ignored, requesting specific variants of the PHP applications, or modifications to the (very basic) nginx proxy configuration I put in front of the website to help with routing, challenge isolation, and logging. It’s possible that if I made further modifications in this vein, more people would’ve been able to solve the challenge. There is no specific evidence to prove that this would be the case.

The second major hosting issue I had is more easily expressed by a video. This is how I exported the WIF private key for my bitcoin wallet that I used in the challenge (Note: the wallet shown here is a different empty wallet. Please don’t use this key since I’ve recorded a video of it online!):

I thought I was putting the key to the wallet in the challenge based on this flow. Turns out I wasn’t. The WIF I exported turned out to be a parent key in a derivation path for the wallet address holding the bitcoin. I’m still not entirely sure which combination of credentials I should’ve provided to make the bitcoin stealable. If I run future challenges of this nature, I’ll probably make the flag the full wallet recovery key instead of any individual private key.

So the winner got the real bitcoin key from the server, but couldn’t use it to move any of the money in the branch wallet derived from that parent key.

Luckily, they reached out over email and provided exceptionally detailed proof including: the full text of the wallet key on the server, its hash, the exact timestamp when they exploited the server, the exact IP address they used to exploit the server, the exact payload they used to exploit the server, AI chat turns from when they developed the exploit, and a full writeup of the exploit they used.

With this information I was able to pull up the full trace in my logs, match down to the second the exploitation time with my logs on the print-flag binary and confirm that they did in fact know the full value of the flag file on the server.

Congrats to the winner for not only solving the challenge, but also solving the secret hidden challenge of keeping excellent exploit logs!

So what did I learn from this experience?

I launched the website out of a degree of skepticism around the breathless reporting of a serious PHP CVE despite a dearth of real-world victims of this attack.

To be honest, I think that was a bad take on my part. PHP2Shell is the real deal. It’s an exploitable vulnerability and a sufficiently motivated adversary, with the help of AI, can absolutely use it to hack a website even when they do not have direct access to memory addresses or the physical server to tailor their exploitation pathway.

If you are running a PHP-based website today, you should absolutely patch PHP2Shell.

I fully expect over the coming months we will see more and more working general purpose exploit chains for PHP2Shell.

If you operate a service that is sufficiently valuable or public enough to warrant specialized attention, my experience with stealmybitcoin.com makes me believe it is a matter of when, not if, someone could target a working PHP2Shell exploit specifically to your system configuration.

On the flip side, I believe stealmybitcoin.com tells us a lot about the current state of AI-assisted cyber exploitation. Out of tens of thousands of people attempting to hack a website with a publicly known (and exploitable!) CVE on it, only two managed to get close to triggering the vulnerability.

While some of the server-side changes I made to make exploitation easier may have had an impact (e.g. the winner solved the challenge about 3 hours after I added php-version.php to the server), many thousands of hackers were unable to trigger the flag binary over the 9-ish hours between the winner’s successful solve and the time when I took the challenge offline.

It’s pretty clear that we aren’t at a time, yet, where an inexpert attacker can take a top LLM + a difficult CVE (like PHP2Shell was) and turn it into a reliable cyber-attack tool.

It does seem that we’re drawing closer to that point every day though. I don’t think there’s any good way to stuff this cat back into the bag, but I do hope that hard work over the coming months across the open source and systems security ecosystem will make it so that hard exploits remain hard.

As someone who has spent a good chunk of my career doing offensive security research, PHP2Shell seems like another example of why enabling good people to find bugs quickly and publicly, so that everyone can get a jump on patching them, is as important as it has ever been.

My interests include cybersecurity, space, software engineering, and policy.

#9864. 'Gheist' Weaponizes GitHub Tokens to Steal Cloud Secrets

An ongoing supply chain attack is harvesting credentials and sensitive data from thousands of developer repositories.

An ongoing attack is abusing compromised GitHub tokens to harvest cloud secrets and credentials from thousands of developer repositories, bringing into focus how compromised developer accounts can provide a gateway into enterprise cloud environments.

Dubbed "Gheist," the campaign has left more than 13,500 malicious branches — or versions of a project's code — across more than 850 compromised GitHub accounts, according to a report published over the weekend by Wiz Research.

The campaign affects everything from personal projects to private enterprise repositories, although public repositories are protected by safeguards GitHub introduced in July, according to the report.

"The control GitHub added is focused on protecting public repositories from workflow abuse vectors," Wiz researcher Rami McCarthy tells Dark Reading. However, "once an enterprise credential is compromised, that control doesn’t apply," he adds.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

Wiz also found overlap between Gheist-affected GitHub accounts and other abuse campaigns, including repository-based malware distribution, attempts to exploit GitHub Actions for computing resources, and possible infections linked to other malware operations.

This overlap — which distinguishes Gheist from similar campaigns — suggests stolen developer tokens may be reused or shared among threat actors, "demonstrating the complexity and activity of this threat landscape," McCarthy says.

The campaign relies on a workflow named "sync-check," which is committed to each repository accessible through a stolen token, the researchers wrote.

"The workflow seeks to print the repository’s secrets into its own workflow log," they wrote. "Then, the tool downloads the log through the GitHub API and deletes the run seconds later. The tool's API requests carry the user agent 'gheist,' which gives the campaign its name."

Wiz began tracking the activity Sept. 15 and said the operation remains active and evolving as of Oct. 24. The researchers reported the activity to GitHub, and about two-thirds of the implicated accounts are no longer available, which "likely indicates response activity," according to the report.

The tokens appear to have come primarily from two sources: infostealer malware and credentials exposed in earlier software supply chain compromises, the researchers noted.

GitHub tokens authorize users and applications to access repositories, code, and administrative functions, making them valuable to attackers seeking to compromise projects and organizations.

Related:Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

Gheist uses stolen GitHub tokens to create branches named "ci-sync-" followed by six characters. The attackers then add the GitHub Actions workflow at .github/workflows/sync-check.yml, using the commit message "ci: sync config," according to the report.

"The commit is unsigned and authored as the token's owner," the researchers wrote. The resulting push event triggers a workflow that attempts to print environment variables and repository secrets into its log. The attack encodes the output using Base32 before retrieving the logs through the GitHub API and deleting the workflow run seconds later.

"Because the secrets leave through GitHub's own API, there is no attacker domain or outbound connection to block," the researchers explained.

A key finding is that Wiz observed successful attacks in private repositories and enterprise environments, where the public-repository safeguard did not apply. Most GitHub-targeted activity, by contrast, primarily affects public repositories, McCarthy tells Dark Reading.

"The attack succeeded in the environments organizations considered safest because a credential issued to a human months ago still carried full write authority," says James Matchett, head of security at supply chain security firm Cloudsmith, in an email interview. "'Private' is not a control. Scoped, short-lived credentials, a tight inventory of what can push and pull, and the discipline to rotate after every incident are the control.”

Related:PapRAT Cyber-Espionage Campaign Leaves a 'Bitter' Taste in South Asia

Wiz observed the attackers cycling through tokens belonging to multiple users and automation accounts, and cloning private repositories before planting malicious workflows. Within hours, cloud credentials from the same organization were used to enumerate AWS Secrets Manager, the researchers added.

Wiz estimates that the campaign affected "on the scale of a dozen companies," McCarthy says. However, "we have not seen consistent or automated abuse outside of mass cloning of GitHub repositories and the core credential theft," he says.

Token abuse is an increasingly common way for attackers to infiltrate organizations through the developer pipeline. Research presented at Black Hat Europe last year found that some of the most significant software supply chain incidents over the preceding year involved threat actors exploiting GitHub flaws. Defenders therefore must treat developer projects as critical organizational assets.

To defend against Gheist and other forms of token abuse, Wiz urged security teams to hunt for malicious GitHub Actions workflows, rotate exposed secrets, and treat compromised self-hosted runners as potential infrastructure breaches.

More specifically, defenders should look for branches named "ci-sync-" followed by six characters, where the only change is a new .github/workflows/sync-check.yml file with the commit message "ci: sync config," the researchers advised. Administrators also should review GitHub audit logs for workflow runs on "ci-sync-*" branches that were deleted within a minute of completion, as well as activity from the user agent "gheist."

For broader protection against GitHub token abuse, Waseem Ahmed, head of engineering at security firm Secure.com, recommends that organizations "replace long-lived personal access tokens with GitHub Apps or short-lived fine-grained tokens" and "require reviewers on any environment that holds production secrets." These measures can help limit attackers' ability to access sensitive credentials even if they obtain valid tokens.

Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#9863. [$] The second part of the 7.4 merge window

The 7.4 merge window, which closed on November 1, included a record-breaking 18,591 non-merge changesets. That is almost as many as the entire 7.3 development cycle, which had 18,765, itself a record breaker. Of those, 11,838 landed after the article covering the first part of the merge window. Most of those were bug fixes of various forms; it seems as though bug fixes may be crowding out feature additions across the open-source ecosystem to some extent. Still, a good number of new features were included, and a handful removed, in the tail end of the merge window.
