#9776. Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

The cybersecurity market is difficult to predict, but a glimpse into the annual DataTribe Challenge shows what's trending and what's not.

Startups have been battling it out on the DataTribe Challenge stage for the past nine years, but this year's event still saw some firsts.

A cyber insurance company made the top five finalists, and attendees got to vote for their favorite finalist with the People's Choice Award. Both of these firsts highlighted how people are looking for answers to new risks introduced by artificial intelligence (AI).

The DataTribe Challenge, hosted by the cyber startup foundry and venture capital firm, is one of the signature events of its annual Cyber Innovation Conference. The meeting, which took place in October, aims to unite the cybersecurity ecosystem, from founders to investors and — since it's held in Washington, D.C. — some policymakers, too.

Cybersecurity conferences pop up on the calendar more frequently these days; that momentum is important "to keep the information fresh" as the industry and threat landscape transforms rapidly, explains Robert Ackerman, co-founder and managing partner at DataTribe. Game-changing incidents that require sharing information emerge almost daily now, he adds, pointing to the more recent PHP2Shell vulnerability that attackers jumped on and proved difficult for organizations to patch.

Related:AI Agents as Insider Threats: Inside Microsoft's Bet on a Unified Security Stack

An expanding pool of cyber-related startups is also driving industry transformation. Nearly 700 rising companies submitted entries or were considered for this year's Challenge, which pairs startups with mentors before they pitch to judges who crown the winner.

As Ackerman and Leo Scott, managing director at DataTribe, filtered down the contestants into the top five list, they found it interesting that many of the startups focused on the dynamics around how AI is driving the market as organizations transition from AI adoption to managing the technology.

Some companies had a more direct tie. This year's winner, Sondera, aims to solve agentic architecture challenges like improving guardrails and security controls.

But cyber insurance company Navasana, which made the top five for the first time ever, was an example of a company indirectly focused on AI. Instead, Navasana launched to handle new risk dynamics that AI created, speaking to broader industry trends.

At one level, everyone's been thinking about cyber insurance for a long time, Ackerman adds. But looking at how policies are written in cyber, he has noticed a shift in risk as they add disclaimers and exemptions.

"What makes cyber attractive from an investment perspective is you never really solve it," Ackerman tells Dark Reading. "You never mitigate risk fully. It's a very hard puzzle piece to put together. The hope with AI is you get this real-time data to understand posture and environments. I still think there's a real lag though because insurance doesn't operate in real time."

Related:RemoteThreat Bets Security Teams Need to Test What Happens After Defenses Fail

Navasna marked the first cyber insurer to make the top five due to the end-to-end, continuous services it offers in a space where organizations manage such a broad umbrella of needs. As an early-stage investor, Ackerman is not looking to "feed the consensus machine" but wants to anticipate what's next. In venture capital, that's hard right now, he adds. Still, the conference and DataTribe Challenge look to showcase companies that are currently topical and addressing real needs.

Navasana is an example of more emerging needs, says Ackerman, while Sondera is in the "sweet spot" by addressing current challenges, as attacks make it clear that agentic AI needs more guardrails.

Sondera is "doing some really interesting things in that space that are well beyond what others are doing," says Scott. What resonated with the audience was how much research Sondera put into understanding what organizations actually need, he adds.

Rather than operating at the rule level, Sondera's approach starts at a much higher level, beginning with the human's underlying intent and what they're trying to achieve. Then organizations can work with users to generate the specific rules.

Related:Deception by Design: CISA's Guide to Tricking Cybercriminals

It's increasingly evident that agents can be very persistent and act independently, so control is essential. That may be one reason that Sondera took home the trophy — people really understand the problems they've seen in their environments, Ackerman adds.

Ackerman sees two timelines in cybersecurity right now. Discussions over the past 18 to 24 months centered around concerns that offense has more of an advantage as attackers use AI to become faster and more advanced. Defense will catch up, but he believes that what the industry knows about cybersecurity — how to protect systems, and layer defense and zero trust — still work.

"We just have to apply them efficiently all the time," he urges.

The other timeline is what happens after 24 months. What issues will emerge then? Those are the core concepts, like protecting Internet infrastructure, that DataTribe wants to showcase in these events.

And the long-term lens is what the investors are betting on right now.

"It's not about what is going to get picked up in the next three to four months," Ackerman says. The startups and investments "have more of a five- to 10-year time horizon," he says.

One of Ackerman's favorite pastimes once startups wrap up their Challenge pitches is to walk around the floor while everyone's waiting for the judges to cast their votes and announce the winner. He considers the disconnect: He has spent weeks with the companies, coaching and prepping, yet the audience full of people from across the industry only get to know them for 20 minutes.

That's what makes storytelling so important, not just the cybersecurity and technical points. Learning what the judges and audience think of these companies is important for DataTribe, as well as for the startups which is the true value of cyber competitions.

For Ackerman, it's always great to hear that people had been thinking about a problem one of the contestants was trying to solve, but no one had developed a solution.

"That's validating," Ackerman says. "We're sort of directionally correct, which maybe in this market is the best you can do on any given day."

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

#9775. PapRAT Cyber-Espionage Campaign Leaves a 'Bitter' Taste in South Asia

Organizations in the region face growing cyberattacks from the known India-linked threat group, which leverages legitimate Windows functionality in three distinct attack chains.

A known South Asian cyber-espionage group has been targeting organizations across the region with attacks designed to compromise Windows systems, establish persistence, and give attackers remote control over infected machines using custom malware.

The attacks, attributed "with high confidence" to the South Asian threat group known as Bitter (aka TA397), involve three distinct infection chains and demonstrate the group's expanding malware capabilities, according to new research from FortiGuard Labs published today.

Bitter, one of several threat groups linked to India, has been active since at least 2013 and has historically targeted government, energy, and engineering organizations. The group is known for using tailored attack campaigns to gain persistent access to victim networks, collect information, and maintain remote control over compromised systems.

At the center of the latest threat campaign is PapRAT, a custom remote access Trojan (RAT) that gives attackers extensive control over compromised Windows systems, including the ability to execute commands, manipulate files, capture screenshots, and download additional payloads, according to FortiGuard Labs.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

"This campaign illustrates how Bitter combines native Windows tools with custom malware to establish and maintain access to targeted systems," Cara Lin, a FortiGuard Labs threat researcher, wrote in the post.

Bitter has recently revamped PapRAT from a C++ code base to Rust, expanding its functionality in the process from eight commands to 11, according to the report. Additional capabilities in the latest version include PowerShell execution, a sleep directive, and a clean-exit command.

"PapRAT's C++ and Rust implementations indicate continued investment in Bitter's toolset," Lin wrote.

Indeed, attackers have increasingly adopted Rust for malware development for various reasons, including its cross-platform development capabilities and potential evasion advantages.

The latest updates to PapRAT also underscore the importance of certain defensive measures, including "monitoring malicious behavior across scripting tools, scheduled tasks, and installer activity alongside detecting known malware signatures," Lin wrote.

Researchers observed three distinct attack chains being used by Bitter, all of which exploit legitimate Windows functionality to disguise malicious behavior.

These tactics demonstrate "how advanced cyberespionage operations deliberately abuse native system tools to evade traditional endpoint detection," notes Shane Barney, chief information security officer at Keeper Security.

Related:Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

The first attack chain uses a malicious LNK file that abuses the native Windows ftp.exe utility to execute scripts and create scheduled tasks that maintain contact with the attackers' command-and-control (C2) server.

The second uses a VHDX disk image containing an LNK file that opens a decoy spreadsheet while silently launching an MSI installer to deploy PapRAT.

The third attack begins with a URL shortcut that retrieves an LNK file through WebDAV, leading to an MSI installer that deploys PapRAT. In this chain, PapRAT also delivers WmRAT, a secondary implant previously documented by other researchers, according to FortiGuard Labs.

"By co-opting native Windows utilities like ftp.exe and scheduled tasks to establish initial command-and-control communication, threat actors operate within trusted administrative channels before deploying custom malware," Barney observes. "When an intrusion leverages trusted system processes, signature-based controls simply have nothing to alert on."

This so-called "hybrid tradecraft," which combines legitimate Windows functionality with custom malware, requires organizations to focus on strict privilege boundaries and identity security rather than relying on endpoint signatures alone as part of a comprehensive defense strategy, Barney says.

Related:Devs Hit by Trojanized Claude Code Extension for Cursor

To defend against these attacks, organizations should treat unexpected LNK files, URL shortcuts, disk images, and MSI packages with caution, particularly when delivered through unsolicited messages, Lin recommended in the post.

"Combining user awareness with controls that detect suspicious execution chains and outbound C2 traffic can help limit exposure to campaigns that blend legitimate Windows functionality with custom malware," she wrote.

The third attack chain is particularly problematic for defenders because removing PapRAT from compromised systems may not eliminate the attacker's access, observes Jason Soroko, senior fellow at Sectigo.

This means defenders need to look deeper into their systems "to check what else was installed and identify scripts and scheduled tasks that could keep fetching commands," he says. A comprehensive recovery effort must look beyond the file that triggered the original alert to identify any additional payloads, persistence mechanisms, or other components of the compromise.

She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. #9774. Data Broker Radaris Loses Domains in Privacy Fight

The radaris.com website, prior to the domain transfer to Atlas.

Less than a month after Atlas sued Radaris, KrebsOnSecurity published a deep dive into the Radaris co-founders — Igor and Dmitry Lubarsky (also spelled Lybarsky) — Russian-born brothers living in Massachusetts who operate a dizzying array of people-search companies as well as a number of Russian language dating services and affiliate programs.

Attorneys for the Lubarsky brothers threatened to sue for defamation if the story wasn’t removed and an apology issued. Their attorney asserted that our reporting was wildly inaccurate, and that the true owners of the company were Ukrainians living in Ukraine.

The Lubarsky brothers Dmitry or “Dan” (left) and Gary/Igor.

KrebsOnSecurity doubled down and showed how the Lubarsky brothers built and operated Radaris and other data broker companies using a fictitious CEO’s name. Our follow-up story noted that Radaris’s attorney — a lawyer with the Boston Law Group named Val Gurvits — admitted his clients had invented the CEO pseudonym “Gary Norden,” and that Radaris also had issued multiple press releases over the years that quoted the fake CEO while seeking money from potential investors.

Attorneys for Radaris waited until the last minute to appear in court and contest what was all but certain to be a default judgment in favor of the plaintiffs, and then told the court that Atlas had failed to serve the real owners and operators of Radaris and several of its sister data broker companies.

Atlas re-filed the lawsuit in June 2025, this time dramatically expanding the number of Radaris family data brokers accused of violating Daniel’s Law. Matt Adkisson, president and CEO of Atlas, said Radaris turned to a tried-and-true playbook: Delaying in court until the last possible minute, and playing shell games with Radaris’s true country of origin and the individuals listed as owners and operators of these sites.

Adkisson said when the defendants updated their terms of service to state that Radaris was suddenly managed by a company in the Marshall Islands, Atlas hired an investigator in that country and soon learned the brand new entity that Radaris claimed was managing the company didn’t even exist yet.

Mr. Gurvits stepped forward as Radaris’s attorney in a class action lawsuit the company temporarily lost in 2017 because it never contested the claim in court. When the plaintiffs told the judge they couldn’t collect on the $7.5 million default judgment, the court ordered the domain registry Verisign to transfer the radaris.com domain name to the plaintiffs.

Mr. Gurvits appealed that verdict, arguing the lawsuit hadn’t named the actual owners of the Radaris domain name — a Cyprus company called Bitseller Expert Limited — and thus taking the domain away would be a violation of their due process rights.

The judge in the 2017 case ruled in Radaris’ favor — halting the domain transfer — and told the plaintiffs they could refile their complaint. Soon after, the operator of Radaris changed from Bitseller to Andtop Company, an entity formed (PDF) in the Marshall Islands in Oct. 2020. The plaintiffs never re-filed their lawsuit.

A mind map of various entities tied to Radaris and the company’s co-founders. Click to enlarge.

“That seemed to be their modus operandi,” said Raj Parikh, a partner at PEM Law in New Jersey who handles most of the Daniel’s Law litigation for Atlas. “In the past, they won by attrition. Plaintiffs’ attorneys tired of the procedural games and just gave up. That strategy worked for a decade, and it probably would have worked in this case too, since any financial recovery from foreign actors will be difficult. But we were acutely aware of the threat this website posed to law enforcement officers and other public officials in New Jersey, and decided early on to commit whatever time and resources were necessary to remove that threat.”

On August 26, the judge in the New Jersey case found the defendants were given multiple chances to appear and defend the claims against them but had failed to do so. Mr. Gurvits declined to comment on the case, saying it had been assigned to another attorney, a Mr. Victor Worms. In response to questions, Mr. Worms asserted the New Jersey court transferred Radaris.com to Atlas as part of a default judgment against Radaris.com, which is not a legal entity.

“We have made a motion to vacate that default judgment on the grounds that it is void since a non-entity has no legal capacity to sue or be sued,” Worms replied. “We also intend to pursue all appropriate appeals because we believe the transfer of Radaris.com amounts to a forfeiture in violation of various constitutional principles.”

While radaris.com still comes up prominently in results when searching online for U.S. residents by name, the domain no longer sells detailed personal dossiers on millions of Americans. Its homepage now displays a notice from Atlas, as well as links to our previous reporting on Radaris.

Atlas told KrebsOnSecurity that it has obtained more than 10,000 emails and documents in the course of litigation, and that those messages confirm our previous reporting on the owners and operators of Radaris and its myriad companies.

Atlas said the emails clearly establish that the nominal legal vehicles — Radaris America, Inc.; Bitseller Expert Limited; Digital Orbit Corp; Core Solutions Group Inc; Lucky Solutions Inc; Virtura Corp; Veripages Inc.; Nuform Solutions Inc.; Growth Data Advisors Inc.; Property Experts, Inc — are all administered by the same three or four people from the same mailboxes, share one bank or payment card set, and are all managed from one virtual office address.

“The corpus establishes, with documentary evidence generated independently by banks, payment processors, hosting providers, registrars, software-as-a-service vendors and the operators’ own systems, that radaris.com and at least twenty-five other people-search websites are one operation run by a small Boston-area group whose administrative, financial and technical functions sit on the difive.com mail domain and its successors (centerex.com, scienteco.com, eprofit.com, realmo.com, pub360.com),” reads a summary shared by Atlas.

Atlas said the emails show Radaris.com earns approximately $42,000 a month, while Veripages.com earns around $45,000 monthly via its partnership with the Lifetime Value Company, a marketing and advertising firm whose brands include PeopleLooker, PeopleSmart, NumberGuru, and Bumper, a car history site.

According to Atlas, the emails also showed the Radaris family of websites earns as much as $25,000 each month from their partnership with Onerep, a company that claims to help people remove their information from people-search sites. In March 2024, KrebsOnSecurity revealed how the Belarusian founder of Onerep had launched and operated dozens of people-search sites over the years and was continuing to operate one of them (Nuwber), effectively spreading the disease and selling the cure.

The domain radaris.com now redirects to this notice from Atlas about the court-ordered domain transfer.

All told, the New Jersey court has so far transferred 14 domain names from the Radaris family of companies to Atlas. Radaris.com now redirects to a notice of the court-ordered domain transfer.

The Radaris family of companies is still potentially facing fines of $1,000 per alleged violation of Daniel’s Law. For the time being, however, Daniel’s Law is facing a constitutional challenge from virtually all of the 150 other consumer data broker firms being sued by Atlas.

The data broker industry responded by having at least 70 of the Atlas lawsuits moved to federal court, challenging the New Jersey statute as overly broad and a violation of the First Amendment. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit has not yet issued a decision on the constitutional challenge, but either way the case is widely expected to be appealed all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court.

Meanwhile, at least 14 other states have now passed laws modeled after the New Jersey statute, with more states considering similar measures. However, West Virginia’s Daniel’s Law was ruled facially unconstitutional under the First Amendment by a federal district court in August 2025.

“These days at the federal level, add in the intense amount of lobbying against these laws from social media companies, big tech, cryptocurrency firms, and now AI proponents in the mix who claim that limiting their data scraping is somehow going to collapse the whole U.S. economy under Chinese rule,” he said.

At least 25 states have passed or implemented laws requiring age verification for residents seeking to access adult content online, but there is no federal law that limits how the companies that are scanning everyone’s drivers license can use, share or keep the data provided. Had such restrictions been enshrined in law, we may have avoided the recent breach at IDScan.net, which exposed the drivers license information on more than 153 million Americans when the records were briefly turned into a point-and-click identity theft service on the dark web.

#9773. Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

#9772. Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

The latest "Digital Defense Report" identifies government agencies as prime targets for AI attacks but doesn't mention that they are broadly being targeted through Microsoft bugs.

AI is changing cybersecurity. The hope is that software will eventually ship with fewer vulnerabilities, while the expectation in the meantime is that vendors will issue eye-popping volumes of software patches as a result of using AI to identify flaws in existing products. Software customers will increasingly use AI to more effectively and efficiently protect their networks. These promising developments will take time to unfold, as vendors and their customers learn how to incorporate AI into their software development and cybersecurity risk management workflows.

Attackers, meanwhile, are already using AI to generate novel attacks and orchestrate increasingly complex and large-scale hacking campaigns. AI is already enabling criminal groups to achieve hacking successes normally reserved for patient, highly resourced nation-state threat actors. And nation-state threat actors are using AI to increase the scale and sophistication of their cyber operations. The threat level is rising at an alarming rate.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

Microsoft flagged the impacts of AI on cybersecurity in its recently released "2026 Digital Defense Report." Among its findings, it assessed that government agencies and services were the most affected by cyber threats and frequently targeted for nation-state activity.

Microsoft's report has a major blind spot, however: the impact of legacy software, especially its own, on organizations' cyber-risk. Legacy software will remain the substrate of organizations' attack surface for the foreseeable future. Vendors need to up their security game, and their customers need to demand better security from their vendors, particularly as AI heightens the threat landscape.

For example, with an 85% market share, Microsoft is the most dominant player in the US public sector productivity software market. Its products are therefore a prime target for state-sponsored groups seeking access to US government agencies and the data and secrets they are charged with protecting. So we should expect attackers to prize vulnerabilities in Microsoft's products and devote a substantial proportion of their hacking efforts to these popular products.

But there is more to the story than Microsoft's sheer prevalence in federal IT. Microsoft's grip on the federal IT market exposes the US government to a disproportionate share of cyber vulnerabilities. According to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Microsoft accounts for nearly 16% of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEVs) so far this year — the most of any company. Microsoft accounts for nearly 23% of known exploited vulnerabilities from November 2021 (when CISA began tracking KEVs) to October 2026.

Related:PapRAT Cyber-Espionage Campaign Leaves a 'Bitter' Taste in South Asia

By comparison, the next-highest vendor, Cisco, is responsible for approximately 7% in 2026 and 6% total, less than half of Microsoft's share.

Some agencies even rely on Microsoft as their single software vendor. This isn't particularly surprising — Microsoft has a track record of locking customers into its ecosystem by bundling its cloud computing offerings with office and security products (bundling is one area of focus of the Federal Trade Commission’s ongoing antitrust investigation into Microsoft) and then making it too difficult or costly for customers to switch vendors.

In 2023, the US Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) discontinued its Data Loss Prevention program after moving to bundle security tools into a sole-source Microsoft enterprise license. The move reportedly put 18 million veterans' personal records at risk of leakage. The VA has now moved to reverse course by seeking alternatives to Microsoft, having recognized the consequences of a Microsoft monoculture. Lesson learned.

Related:Devs Hit by Trojanized Claude Code Extension for Cursor

Microsoft's Digital Defense Report identifies how frequently government agencies are affected by cyber threats and targeted for nation-state activity. Microsoft knows this firsthand. Since 2023, Chinese state-sponsored actors have compromised Microsoft products in at least two significant instances, accessing over two dozen US government agencies' emails in one attack and compromising at least seven agencies in another in July 2025.

Russian state-backed actors have also exploited Microsoft's weak security at least three times since 2020, including the infamous SolarWinds attack and an operation to exfiltrate emails between Microsoft personnel and government agencies. US government officials and advisory bodies have concluded that these breaches were preventable and caused by Microsoft's negligence. The reach and severity of breaches will only grow as China, Russia, and other nation-state threat actors become AI-native and AI tools become increasingly sophisticated.

Microsoft deserves some credit for using AI to evaluate products it has already deployed: its record-setting Patch Tuesday count of 974 vulnerabilities disclosed last month is no doubt the result of using AI to identify flaws. But that's not good enough.

All software vendors, including Microsoft, should invest more in the security of their products before they are released, even if it comes at the expense of slowing the rollout of new product features. And they should all be transparent to customers about these processes to enable customers to make more informed purchasing decisions. Otherwise, Microsoft's "2027 Digital Defense Report" will paint an even darker picture of the threat environment.

Director of the Program on Geopolitics, Technology, and Governance, Stanford University

Andrew Grotto founded and directs the Program on Geopolitics, Technology, and Governance at Stanford University's Center for International Security and Cooperation. He serves as the faculty lead for the Cyber Policy and Security specialization in Stanford’s master’s in international policy program, where he teaches courses on cyber policy and economic statecraft. He is also a visiting fellow at the Hoover Institution. Previously, he was senior advisor to the Secretary of Commerce for technology policy during the Obama administration and Senior Director for Cyber Policy on the National Security Council in the Obama and Trump administrations. He advises technology companies on digital risks, including companies that compete with Microsoft.

#9771. AI Doom or AI Bubble? What to Actually Expect from AI in the Next Two Years

If you follow AI news, you’ve probably noticed two stories running side by side. In one, AI is so powerful that it may wipe out humanity within a few years. In the other, AI is wildly overhyped and the money pouring into it is a bubble about to burst. Even Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, has said investors are “overexcited” about AI.

Both stories can’t be fully true at once. Either AI is about to become all-powerful, or it’s a lot less impressive than the valuations suggest. I work with tech companies on content and strategy, and I kept hearing smart people repeat one headline or the other. So I went looking for a more grounded view.

One of the most level-headed takes I came across was from Denis Stebunov, CEO of the software development company ivelum, who recently recorded his thoughts on these headlines. His view, which I’ll lean on throughout this piece, is that the doomsday scenario and the bubble panic both miss what’s actually going on with AI, and what we should expect from it over the next couple of years.

It’s natural to feel uneasy about AI. It’s new, it moves fast, and few people fully understand how it works. Anxiety about the unknown is a very human reaction. But Stebunov argues there’s more to the doomsday narrative than ordinary nerves.

The first factor is old and well documented: bad news sells. Open any news site and the headlines are about wars, hurricanes, crashes, and crimes. Plenty of good things happen too; they just don’t get the clicks. “Bad news drive more engagement,” as Stebunov puts it. “People are more likely to click on something that sparks anxiety.” A study published in Nature Human Behaviour analyzed about 105,000 headline variations tested on the news site Upworthy and found that each additional negative word in a headline raised the click-through rate by about 2.3%.

The second factor is less obvious. The warnings about AI’s dangers don’t only come from random people online. They come from the leading AI companies, which talk to the public and to governments about risks and regulation. In Stebunov’s view, raising these concerns has become part of the PR strategy of the two largest AI labs, OpenAI and Anthropic. A product that might be dangerous is, by implication, a very powerful product. “It’s a bold move,” he says, “and it’s clearly working.”

The third factor is cultural. Most of us grew up on The Terminator and The Matrix, which paint a vivid picture of machines taking over. More hopeful visions exist, Star Trek among them, but they don’t stick the same way. So when someone mentions very advanced AI, most people picture Skynet, a story they already know.

None of this means AI is harmless. Stebunov has concerns of his own, and the most concrete is cybersecurity.

The threat is no longer hypothetical. In November 2025, Anthropic reported that it had disrupted a cyber-espionage campaign by a state-sponsored group that used its AI model to attack roughly 30 organizations. The AI carried out 80 to 90% of the tactical work on its own, according to the report, with humans stepping in mainly to approve the big decisions.

But the same technology works on defense. In July 2025, Google said its AI agent Big Sleep had found a critical vulnerability in SQLite, a widely used open-source database, that attackers were preparing to exploit. Google called it the first time an AI agent had directly foiled an exploitation attempt in the wild.

“It’s more like a cat-and-mouse game,” Stebunov says, “which probably will be accelerating.” Attackers get faster, defenders get faster, and organizations that don’t keep up will pay for it. That’s a serious problem, and a very different one from the end of humanity.

In fairness, the doomsayers are mostly not talking about today’s AI. They mean future systems that will be far more capable, and their argument goes: look how much progress AI made in the past few years, and imagine where it will be in a few more.

“This is a classic extrapolation,” Stebunov says. You take the past trend and assume it will continue at the same pace, or faster. That’s a reasonable starting point, but only if you understand where the past progress came from.

The technology behind today’s chatbots goes back to 2017, when researchers at Google introduced the transformer architecture. In 2018, OpenAI built on it with GPT, the generative pre-trained transformer. That was the scientific breakthrough.

What followed, in Stebunov’s words, was “not a series of scientific breakthroughs, but rather scaling of the same idea.” The industry discovered that the bigger the model and the more it’s trained, the better it performs. That’s where most of the money went: bigger models, more compute, more data centers.

There were also two important advances in how the models are used. First, they learned to use tools. Second came agents, which run the model in a loop with the right tools and context so it can work through a task step by step. “That was big,” Stebunov says. “Agents can now perform real tasks, and this has already changed how people work.”

Still, the research itself produced no new fundamental breakthrough. Ilya Sutskever, one of OpenAI’s co-founders, has made the same point. He has described 2012 to 2020 as the age of research and 2020 to 2025 as the age of scaling, and argued that making models a hundred times bigger won’t transform everything. In his view, the field is heading back to research.

If most recent progress came from scaling, the question is how long scaling can continue. Not forever, Stebunov says, though nobody knows when it will slow down. “Maybe it will plateau in the next year, or maybe not.”

A genuine new breakthrough would change the picture, and he isn’t aware of one on the horizon. Without it, his forecast is refreshingly unexciting: “We’ll probably have more or less the same, just better, and with more practical applications.”

In practice, that means steady improvement rather than leaps: models that keep getting better at reasoning, coding, and following instructions. The biggest gains will come from putting the existing models to work in narrow, well-defined areas where agents can handle real tasks. And much of the change will come from more companies figuring out how to use what already exists, rather than from smarter models arriving.

That’s a long way from superintelligence by 2028, and a long way from a technology about to collapse.

The bubble worry isn’t made up. In August 2025, Sam Altman told reporters: “Are we in a phase where investors as a whole are overexcited about AI? My opinion is yes.”

The numbers explain the nerves. According to Futurum Group, the five largest US cloud and AI infrastructure companies planned to spend roughly $660 to $690 billion on capital expenditure in 2026, nearly double the year before. OpenAI ended 2025 with about $20 billion in annualized revenue, and Futurum estimated that all pure-play AI vendors together would bring in under $35 billion in 2026, a small fraction of what’s going into infrastructure.

So a correction is entirely possible. But a bubble is about valuations and expectations, not about whether the underlying technology is useful. The dot-com crash is the obvious comparison. When it hit in 2000, the Nasdaq lost most of its value and many companies disappeared. The internet didn’t. It went on to reshape almost every industry, and some of the survivors became the giants of today.

Stebunov makes a similar point about AI. OpenAI and Anthropic may have the best technology today, but they’re far from the only players: there are open-weight Chinese models, Mistral in Europe, Google, xAI, and others. Even if some of the most expensive bets fail, the models already exist, and many of them can be downloaded and run by anyone. “The technology proved its usefulness,” he says. “It is here to stay.”

If neither the apocalypse nor the crash is the main story, what is? For Stebunov, the answer is work, and his own industry is in the front line. “While I don’t believe that AI will wipe out humanity,” he says, “I think it may wipe out some jobs, particularly in the software development industry.” And that will happen whether or not the bubble bursts.

That’s where the conversation about AI is worth having: which tasks AI takes over, which skills become more valuable, and how companies should adapt.

Stebunov describes himself as fairly optimistic about AI, and after looking into it, so am I. We have a remarkable new technology that, like every technology before it, can be used for good and for harm. The risks are real, but they’re specific and manageable, and they look nothing like the movies.

The bubble may or may not burst. Either way, AI will keep improving step by step and finding its way into more of the work we do. That’s less thrilling than the headlines and more useful to plan for.

As Stebunov puts it: “We humans are extremely adaptable. We survived the ice age, and I’m sure we’ll figure out how to deal with AI.”

The Model Is the Easy Part: What Actually Breaks When AI Goes to Production

#9769. U.S. Soldier Gets 70 Months in Prison for AT&T, Verizon Extortions

A U.S. Army soldier who pleaded guilty to hacking into multiple telecommunications companies and stealing mobile call and text metadata for more than 100 million AT&T customers in 2024 was sentenced to 70 months in federal prison today and ordered to pay nearly $300,000 in restitution to victims.

One of several selfies from the Facebook page of Cameron Wagenius.

Cameron John Wagenius, 22, was stationed at a U.S. Army base in South Korea when he adopted the cybercriminal persona “Kiberphant0m.” Working with three alleged co-conspirators, Kiberphant0m downloaded data from several large customers of the cloud data storage service Snowflake that had exposed credentials and did not enforce multi-factor authentication (Snowflake has since mandated MFA on all accounts).

In October 2024, Kiberphant0m bragged on the cybercrime forums that he’d stolen the call and text metadata (e.g. source and destination number, timestamp, duration, etc.) for tens of millions of AT&T customers. Kiberphant0m claimed to have hacked into more than dozen telecommunications companies worldwide, including Verizon’s Push-to-Talk business, and publicly extorted these companies in exchange for a promise not to publish the stolen data.

In late November 2025, KrebsOnSecurity warned that Kiberphant0m was likely a U.S. soldier stationed in South Korea. Less than a month later, Wagenius was arrested and charged in two separate federal indictments, and soon pleaded guilty to all counts in both cases.

At his sentencing hearing in Seattle today, Wagenius was sentenced to nearly six years in federal prison, and ordered to pay $294,978 in restitution.

Federal prosecutors said Wagenius was assisted in his efforts to extort victim companies by Kenneth Schuchman, a 28-year old man from Vancouver, Washington who has a lengthy cybercriminal history. In 2019, Schuchman pleaded guilty to operating the Satori botnet, a vast collection of hacked Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices that was used for large-scale distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks.

Two other alleged co-conspirators of Wagenius are still facing charges in connection with the Snowflake data thefts; Conor Riley Moucka, a.k.a. “Judische,” of Kitchener, Ontario was arrested in 2024 and pleaded guilty in August 2026; and John Erin Binns, an American man currently living in Turkey who is also wanted for a 2021 data breach at T-Mobile that exposed the personal information of at least 76 million customers.

Kiberphant0m also admitted to re-extorting victims, and threatening to disclose national security secrets. Immediately following Moucka’s arrest — after AT&T had already paid the extortion group a $370,000 Bitcoin ransom — Kiberphant0m posted on hacker forums what he claimed were the AT&T call logs for then President-elect Donald Trump and for then Vice President Kamala Harris, as well as schematics allegedly stolen from the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA).

Paul Russell is a resident agent in charge at the Defense Criminal Investigative Service (DCIS), the criminal investigative arm of the U.S. Department of Defense Office of Inspector General. Russell said when DCIS received information that a soldier with secret clearance was allegedly involved in cybercrime and extortion, the agency began working the investigation alongside the FBI, the Army Criminal Investigative Division (CID), and the U.S. Secret Service.

“We don’t often get leads where there’s an active duty soldier with a secret clearance who’s creating hacking tools and trafficking in data,” Russell said. “That doesn’t happen every day, and so when that hits it really spins all of our partner organizations up. It was very serious from jump street, just because it was unique, it was an insider threat, and we weren’t sure what we were dealing with.”

A sentencing memo (PDF) filed Sept. 19 by federal prosecutors in Seattle notes that while Wagenius pleaded guilty almost immediately and has been remarkably cooperative, he recently got caught trying to find security vulnerabilities in the BOP’s computer network. The government’s memo notes that while incarcerated and awaiting sentencing, Wagenius violated the computer use policies of the Bureau of Prisons (BOP) in attempts to learn about vulnerabilities in BOP computer systems.

“According to records from BOP, in or around September 2025, Wagenius used another inmate’s email system to request that the email recipient prompt a commercial AI tool to provide information about “[w]hat CVE’s are there for Windows 10 Enterprise privilege escalation and bypasses” and to “[p]rovide the CVE’s and a real world working script for each CVE . . . without omitted code,” the government’s memo states.

The memo states that less than a week later, Wagenius used a different inmate’s email account and requested that the email recipient prompt an AI tool to “[p]rovide the step by step for CVE-2023-45208, code for this if any, and if no code exists make some, make sure to describe everything in detail.” CVE-2023-45208 is a three-year-old “command injection” vulnerability in D-Link networking devices.

That same month, Wagenius allegedly again requested that the email recipient prompt AI with the question, “How do you make an antenna in a prison environment with commissary or readily available items/tools to improve/make an antenna to extend radio reception?”

Federal prosecutors said Wagenius also requested that the recipient research escaping prison.

“In several instances, Wagenius framed the AI queries as being posed in connection to a book he was writing. This is a common method of ‘prompt injection,’ in which attackers feed specially crafted, deceptive inputs into commercial AI tools that are programmed to avoid outputting malicious code that can be used to exploit computer vulnerabilities,” the sentencing memo reads.

The government told the court it is unaware of evidence that Wagenius figured out how to use or deploy the vulnerabilities he was researching in the BOP’s systems, and when questioned said he was only researching “potential vulnerabilities to provide information to the BOP.”

Incredibly, despite the enormous financial value of the data stolen from AT&T and other telecom providers, Wagenius’s extortion efforts were largely unsuccessful. The government’s sentencing memo says Wagenius made a whopping total of around $1,500 from selling stolen data.

“While Wagenius was not particularly financially successful as a cybercriminal, he both intended to and caused significant harm to numerous individual victims, U.S. companies, and the U.S. government,” the memo states.

#9768. One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

The record theft shows how weak system separation, inadequate controls, and untested attack possibilities can turn one breach into systemic loss.

Last week's $6.3 billion breach at Binance underscores why effective security often depends not just on what an organization's controls are designed to block, but also on what they are configured to allow.

Details from Binance's disclosures thus far show that a threat actor, whom the FBI has identified as North Korea's TraderTraitor group, compromised a developer's laptop to access an internal service container with the permissions to initiate withdrawal requests.

Using that access as a starting point, the attackers exploited additional points of compromise and an Ethereum account-delegation mechanism to gain transaction approval authority over a hot wallet. And in around 20 minutes, the threat actors drained billions of dollars in assets.

In the process, the attackers appear to have bypassed Binance's normal approval controls. The company itself has said there's no evidence the attackers used any leaked wallet keys to carry out the massive theft.

Related:Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

"Binance's initial findings pointed to a compromised laptop belonging to an employee as the starting point. Its subsequent investigation has identified additional points of breach, showing the incident went beyond one device," the cryptocurrency exchange noted.

The incident, at least based on available details so far, has raised questions about whether Binance had sufficient independent safeguards to prevent a compromised system from approving and executing unauthorized withdrawals.

"At a minimum, a platform holding digital assets should have multiple layers of security so no single compromise, such as a hacked employee laptop, can authorize a transfer," says Tim Rawlins, senior adviser and director of security at NCC Group. "Those layers need to be independent of one another."

Funds, for instance, should be separated across hot and cold wallets to limit the impact of a compromise. Developers and administrators should have privileged access workstations to ensure systems they used for critical operations are separate from those they use for other activities such as email and Web browsing, he says. Also critical is 24/7 monitoring for anomalous behavior to help detect compromised endpoints and suspicious activity before attackers can exploit privileged access.

The focus should be on identifying single points of compromise, such as components or privileged roles whose compromise could give an attacker control over funds. "Protecting private keys is only part of the challenge. The systems that request and approve their use must also be secured. A properly secured system has layered, independent controls, hot/cold separation, and has been through threat modelling and end-to-end security testing," Rawlins says.

Related:PapRAT Cyber-Espionage Campaign Leaves a 'Bitter' Taste in South Asia

For now, much remains unclear about exactly how the unauthorized transactions occurred and what safeguards Binance had in place to protect against them. Following the attack, the cryptocurrency exchange moved quickly to freeze some $3 billion. It has also claimed to have replenished — though not recovered — approximately 95% of the affected assets, meaning it has used its own funds to replace the stolen assets.

Cryptocurrency exchanges face many of the same threats as traditional financial institutions. But unlike banks and other financial institutions, which have long been subject to regulations governing operational risk and security, crypto exchanges have not yet faced the same level of oversight, making them a popular target for attackers.

John Bruggeman, vCISO at IT services firm CBTS, says large cryptocurrenct exchanges like Binance have to know that they are constantly being targeted by threat actors. In addition to controls that protect the perimeter or authenticate users, these companies also need to know what trusted identities and systems can do, verify high-impact actions, and prevent one compromised component from becoming a path to valuable assets.

Related:Devs Hit by Trojanized Claude Code Extension for Cursor

That means segregation of duties, management of private keys that authorize transfers, limits on the size of a transfer, MFA on the use of the private key monitoring, alerting for large transfers, and endpoint detection on all employee devices, Bruggeman says.

Also key is user behavior analysis for all users. Architecturally, organizations like Binance should have custody mechanisms for protecting the cryptocurrency and wallets themselves, transaction controls on how to move the cryptocurrency, some kind of rate limits on withdrawals, identity and access controls, and segregation of duties so no one user can initiate and also finalize a transfer, Bruggeman says.

The Binance breach is an important reminder of why all organizations need to test the path that attackers can potentially take after gaining initial access to an environment and not assume that individual controls, each working as they should, are sufficient protection, analysts said. "The entry point and the damage can sit very far apart, so stop grading your security by how well the front door holds," says Waseem Ahmed, head of engineering at Secure.com.

The traditional approach to security is to check whether a request is valid. It almost never checks whether the action behind it should happen, he says. Available information suggests the attackers used Binance's own signing system to sign the transfers, so they looked valid on the way out. It was the "correct math, wrong decision," Ahmed says.

Security has to move from proving identity to governing consequences, he says. That means putting a human approval gate in front of any action that moves money or data, with limits that count across every system at once. "And test the whole route from laptop to payout, not each box on its own," Ahmed advises.

The Binance attack scenario can play out in any enterprise, too. "Swap out the withdrawal service for a payment system, a customer database, or a deployment pipeline, and this is an ordinary enterprise breach," he says. "A clean report from every tool you own tells you nothing about whether someone can walk from a laptop to the money, because no single tool is asked that question."

Robert Coles, senior manager of threat intelligence security at Black Duck, says the broader takeaway for organizations isn't really about cryptocurrency or the attack on Binance itself. Rather, it's about the blast radius, or what happens after initial break-in. It's one thing, he says, for an attacker to gain initial access. But turning that into a theft of billions of dollars is another entirely.

"Every organization has critical systems and privileged accounts where a compromise can have a much bigger impact," Coles says. "We spend a lot of time asking how we keep attackers out. We should spend just as much time asking, ‘If they do get in, what stops them next?'"

Security teams must assume something eventually will get compromised and make sure that one compromise doesn't become a catastrophic business event, Coles noted.

The Binance breach, the biggest ever by magnitude, is by no means the first to affect a major cryptocurrency exchange. In February 2025, Bybit lost approximately $1.5 billion in cryptocurrency after attackers manipulated a transaction approval process involving an Ethereum cold wallet. In May 2019, Binance itself lost 7,000 bitcoin after attackers obtained user API keys and two-factor authentication codes to bypass existing security checks. In October this year, attackers compromised a third-party script on Polymarket's website and used it to move funds from some user wallets.

North Korean threat actors have been especially aggressive in targeting crypto exchanges and wallets in general and account for 76% of all the money that traders have reported as stolen so far in 2026. In six of the past nine years, groups from the cash-strapped nation have accounted for at least one-third of all reported cryptocurrency theft.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9767. Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:

Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.
